summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted to install electric vehicle charging stations at a Huntingdonshire shopping centre, replacing existing parking spaces. The application, lodged by InstaVolt Ltd, proposes four rapid charging stations for electric cars in the King James Retail Centre car park off Ermine Street in Godmanchester, near Huntingdon. The plan includes one fully accessible charging bay and associated equipment. Covering an area of approximately 122 square metres, the development site is currently used for customer parking. Six existing standard parking spaces would be replaced by four rapid electric vehicle charging stations under the plans. The applicant, Ashwin Eapen, acting on behalf of InstaVolt Ltd, states that the company operates more than 2,500 rapid chargers already in service or under construction across the UK. The company also notes that all electricity supplied through its charging network comes from certified renewable sources. InstaVolt claims that the additional charging infrastructure is needed to support the continued growth of electric vehicle ownership and to help meet national net-zero targets. The company also says that the development would contribute to improved air quality, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, and the wider decarbonisation of transport. The proposal includes charging units, a feeder pillar, CCTV equipment, associated cabling and line marking, including green-painted markings for the accessible bay. The application will be decided by Huntingdonshire District Council at a future date. Full details on the application can be found using the Huntingdonshire planning portal with reference 26/01647/FUL.

metadata.title: Award honours local businesses accelerating net zero goals
metadata.contentSnippet: Find out more about the award criteria for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027's Net Zero Award, sponsored by Ørsted.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Award honours local businesses accelerating net zero goals
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Entries are open for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027's Net Zero Award, sponsored by Ørsted. The winner of the Net Zero Award will be an organisation that is making significant progress towards net zero emissions, demonstrating a clear understanding of their current carbon impact and strategies to reduce it. “Entrants for the Net Zero Award should have already analysed their impacts, made clear plans to achieving net zero and have tangible results to demonstrate,” said Luke Bridgman, managing director of award sponsor Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm. “They won’t necessarily have completed their journey, but they will be a good way down the path.” Mr Bridgman explained how entrants’ net zero ambitions should be “authentic”, with clear targets, strategies to meet them and buy-in from senior management. “One person should have ownership of the net zero strategy and be supported at board or CEO level,” he added. “Entrants should be able to show clear results with an explanation of how their strategy helped to achieve them.” Luke Bridgman, managing director of Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 wind farm (Image: Matthew Usher Photography) Entering the Net Zero Award will challenge companies to examine their existing strategies and reflect on what has worked and what hasn’t. They will be able to show clear evidence of how, throughout this journey, they have collaborated with partners. They will also showcase measurable carbon reductions and, perhaps most importantly, innovation – something which Mr Bridgman said is “vital to create the green energy systems of tomorrow”. The winner will be recognised by peers, customers and the wider community as an inspirational business that is actively contributing to a greener future. “It should also boost morale within their organisation and lead to even greater involvement from staff and suppliers with their net zero ambitions,” Mr Bridgman said. “Ultimately it should give businesses an even greater incentive to push towards the net zero goal.” Submit your entries before the deadline on Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information about the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To read about all of the award categories, please click here. Meet the sponsor Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm will deliver enough green energy to power more than 3.3 million UK homes. An £8.5 billion infrastructure project, Hornsea 3 is a cornerstone of the UK government’s climate and clean energy targets and will make a significant contribution toward UK energy security, as well the local and national economy. Located 120km off the Norfolk coast and 160km off the Yorkshire coast, Hornsea 3 is Ørsted’s third gigawatt-scale project in the Hornsea zone, which it has been developing since 2015. Globally, Ørsted is the market leader in offshore wind and was the first energy company in the world to have its science-based net-zero emissions target validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). The judges will be seeking an organisation that has made significant progress toward achieving or maintaining net zero emissions. Innovation, measurable carbon reductions, and collaboration with partners will be key factors. The scalability and potential for other organisations to adopt similar strategies will also be considered.

metadata.title: Man arrested after young boy thrown into crocodile pit has bail extended
metadata.contentSnippet: Police have issued a major update on the man accused of throwing a three-year-old boy into a zoo's crocodile enclosure.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man arrested after young boy thrown into crocodile pit has bail extended
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have issued an update on a man who was arrested after a three-year-old boy was thrown into a zoo's crocodile pit. The toddler was rushed to hospital in critical condition after he ended up in the enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon, on June 18. He had been treated at the scene after he was rescued by staff members, including the zoo's owners Andy and Tracey Johnson. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder but released just hours later. A 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and released on bail (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) He was assessed by detectives as being unfit for interview and released on police bail until Friday (September 18). However, in an update today (Monday, September 14) Cambridgeshire Constabulary confirmed the man has been re-bailed until December 17. More than £117,000 has been raised by the toddler who returned home after spending more than a month in hospital. His parents detailed the horrific injuries he sustained, including tendon and nerve damage, broken bones and severe tissue damage. Police declared a critical incident after the toddler sustained serious injuries (Image: SWNS) It was later revealed the boy was attacked by a crocodile when he ended up in the enclosure, the force confirmed. A source with knowledge of the situation claimed the man, believed to have learning difficulties, was visiting the zoo with two carers. It is alleged the carers left the crocodile enclosure with the suspect after the incident but were stopped by staff members. Norfolk County Council launched an investigation into whether the man is being neglected or abused while in care. The local authority revealed it had launched a Section 42 inquiry and stopped referrals to the care provider in the suspect's case. More than £117,000 has been raised for the toddler who has been discharged from hospital (Image: SWNS) While the suspect is from the county, it is understood his care was not commissioned, provided or paid for by the council. Johnsons of Old Hurst described the incident as "one of the most distressing" in its history. The zoo thanked visitors who "stepped forward to help," including off-duty paramedics and police officers. It was confirmed no safety concerns were indicated regarding the zoo's conditions at the time of the incident. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: School council creates banner urging safer parking outside Hunts primary school
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers dropping children at a Huntingdonshire school have been warned about their bad parking, which is putting pupils and other road users at risk. The school council at Round House Primary Academy in St Neots recently debated parents parking on double yellow lines and blocking the one-way road. Rhys Thomas, a Year 4 teacher and the council’s staff facilitator, said the school had previously tackled the parking problem with letters to parents and carers. He said the parking improves briefly after the letters are sent, but soon returns. Read more District council to move forward with local plan despite calls to pause it Ex-Cambs officer drove police vehicle while under the influence of alcohol Plans to ‘reimagine’ bus services across Cambridgeshire MP wades in amid claims migrants being housed in Huntingdonshire Progress update on £329m A141 and St Ives transport scheme Now the young councillors have designed and commissioned a sign urging drivers to park considerately and stay off the double yellow lines on the narrow street. The banner at the school entrance states: "Keep us safe! Do not park on the double yellow lines." Rhys said the children asked Business Printing Company to donate towards the banner, but the firm provided it for free. "We know parents are parking on the double yellow lines for convenience at drop off and pick up times, but they need to consider the safety of the pupils, and also other road users who find it difficult to get through," said Rhys. He said a photo of the banner was posted on the school’s social media with the message about the poor parking, and it seemed to have had a positive effect. "We have noticed that fewer people are parking on the double yellow lines and are using the car park instead; we just hope that continues," he said. Police previously said they would warn parents before issuing £30 fines for inconsiderate parking outside primary schools in St Neots.

metadata.contentSnippet: Plans for a landmark community building in Northstowe aim to bring together health, library and community services.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans for a landmark community building bringing together health, library and community services have been submitted in Cambridgeshire. South Cambridgeshire District Council has applied to build the Northstowe Town Hub, which would become the growing town’s focal point if approved. Known as Wayfinder, the four-storey building would be located between the future High Street and Town Plaza and provide more than 4,000 square metres of flexible space. The hub is designed to bring a wide range of services together under one roof, including healthcare facilities, a library, community spaces and a café. Dr Lisa Redrup, councillor responsible for healthy communities, said: "Submitting this planning application marks another important milestone towards the creation of Northstowe's civic heart. CGI - The atrium view at the Northstowe Town Hub (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) "If approved, the Town Hub will bring together health, learning and community services in a modern, accessible and sustainable building, creating a welcoming destination for residents of all ages." The plans include more than 1,290 square metres for GP and other healthcare services, plus a pharmacy facing the High Street. A modern library would feature dedicated areas for children, teenagers and adult learners, as well as quiet study spaces and collaborative working environments. CGI - The atrium view at the Northstowe Town Hub (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) The proposals also include a large community hall, meeting rooms, workspaces, a café, landscaped terraces and a full-height atrium intended to serve as an internal meeting place and performance space. The name Wayfinder was inspired by a historic trig point that once stood on the site. The council says the original metalwork will be reinstated at its exact coordinates, while discussions are taking place about transforming the trig pillar into a sculpture. Plan - The exterior view at the Northstowe Town Hub (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) The design draws on the surrounding fen landscape, local aviation history and traditional Cambridgeshire architecture. Environmental features would include green roofs, energy-efficient technology and measures to support wildlife. Councillor Natalie Warren-Green said: "The Town Hub would provide a welcoming place where people can access healthcare, support, learning opportunities and community activities closer to home. "It has the potential to become a real focal point for the community and an important part of everyday life in Northstowe." A public consultation on the plans is now under way before the application is determined.

metadata.title: Column: Mayor reflects on busy month supporting Huntingdon community
metadata.contentSnippet: The Mayor of Huntingdon, Cllr Patrick Kadewere, writes his monthly column.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Column: Mayor reflects on busy month supporting Huntingdon community
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Mayor of Huntingdon, Cllr Patrick Kadewere, writes his monthly column The summer months are always a busy time for community events, and August has been no exception. From celebrations of inclusion and diversity to discussions about the future of our high street, I have had the pleasure of attending a wide range of events that highlight the strength and vibrancy of our communities. This month, I was delighted to attend the Dance Ability Summer Ball at the Montagu Club. It was a wonderful celebration of inclusion, friendship, and community spirit, and a pleasure to see so many people enjoying themselves. My mayoral duties have also taken me beyond Huntingdon, including visits to the March Armed Forces Fair, feeding the meerkats at Hamerton Zoo as part of their Summer Fayre, and enjoying the Cirquoise at Johnson's of Old Hurst. Visit - Mayor of Huntingdon, Patrick Kadewere, and Mayoress Marion Kadewere feeding the meerkats at Hamerton Zoo (Image: Patrick Kadewere) One particularly memorable occasion was attending A Night of African Elegance 2026 in Peterborough. During the evening, I was deeply touched to receive a surprise Certificate of Honour in recognition of my work within the community. The presentation was completely unexpected, and I accepted it with great pride and humility. While the award was presented to me personally, I see it as a reflection of the many people, organisations, and volunteers who work tirelessly to support our communities every day. Closer to home, I have also begun a new business engagement initiative, with the aim of visiting as many Huntingdon businesses as possible during my mayoral year. My first visits included The Lark Coffee & Bar, Molby's, and STS Tyre Pros. Award - Patrick Kadewere receiving a Certificate of Honour at the Night of African Elegance (Image: Patrick Kadewere) I look forward to continuing these visits in the months ahead, listening to business owners, celebrating their successes, and understanding how we can work together to support our town. It has also been a busy month for the Town Council. Alongside our monthly Full Council meeting, councillors have continued to consider planning issues through the Planning Committee, including proposals brought forward by Capital & Centric. These discussions are an important part of ensuring that the views of residents are represented as Huntingdon continues to grow and develop. Whether attending community events, visiting local businesses, or participating in council meetings, I am continually reminded of the passion people have for Huntingdon and the many ways they contribute to making it a great place to live, work, and visit.

Planning committees across Cambridgeshire are handling a steady stream of applications and appeals. We’ve picked out applications that are pending or have been decided on across the area over the last month which we think you should know about. Initial plans have been submitted for a huge storage and distribution development on land north of Cambridge Road, in Fenstanton. An Environmental Impact Assessment scoping report was submitted to Huntingdonshire District Council on September 2. An outline application proposes up to 100,000 square metres of industrial, storage and distribution space. The 10 hectare site would sit on the edge of Fenstanton (Image: Pegasus Group) The plans also include commercial, business, industrial, storage and distribution uses, plus car and HGV parking. The development would include transport links for pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles. The junction of London Road and St Ives Road would also be converted into a roundabout to serve the site. Plans for 13 new homes on the site of a former social club near the Princess of Wales Hospital in Ely have been approved. The site was once part of the hospital, providing staff and visitor parking before a social club was built there. The club has since been demolished. Plans for the 13 new homes near the Princess of Wales Hospital in Ely have been approved (Image: Gary Johns Architects) The plans include a two-storey block of one- and two-bedroom flats as well as two- and three-bedroom houses. Ely City Council opposed the proposals and recommended refusal because of “the loss of public amenity” and “loss of green space”. One local resident said they would object, adding: “we simply don't need more housing being developed in this area.” Plans have been submitted to turn an empty village pub into a school for pupils with special educational needs. The Sage School has applied to turn the vacant George pub in Doddington into a school for pupils aged 11 to 18. The school would expand The Sage School’s existing specialist provision in March. The George, in Doddington, could be converted into a school for SEND pupils (Image: Street View) It would create places for young people who cannot be supported in mainstream schools. The George has struggled to remain a viable pub for several years. Wisbech-based Elgood’s Brewery owns the building and is still marketing it as a tenancy opportunity. But the site has been difficult to lease and has no secured long-term future as a licensed pub. A village chapel left empty for years will reopen as a café and co-working space. The Methodist Chapel in Tydd St Giles opened in 1886 but was last used in 2015, according to applicant DND Core. It said the building had been left “in a state of decay” with “dry rot throughout the timber ground floor, which has collapsed in part”. The plans originally included three parking spaces but were reduced to two to stop cars overhanging the footpath. The Methodist Chapel opened in 1886 but was last used in 2015 (Image: Street View) Eight cycle parking spaces were also included. Tydd St Giles Parish Council unanimously backed the plans, calling them a “good use of a redundant building in the heart of the village”. The new café and co-working space was approved to open from 8am to 9pm Monday to Saturday. It will also open from 8am to 5pm on Sundays and bank holidays. South Cambridgeshire District Council applied to build the Northstowe Town Hub, which would become the growing town’s focal point if approved. The four-storey Wayfinder building would stand between the future High Street and Town Plaza. South Cambridgeshire District Council hopes to build the Northstowe Town Hub (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) The plans include more than 1,290 square metres for GP and other healthcare services, plus a pharmacy facing the High Street. The design draws on the local landscape, local aviation history and traditional Cambridgeshire architecture. Environmental features would include green roofs, energy-efficient technology and wildlife measures. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.contentSnippet: Love exploring National Trust sites and fancy a nice walk with plenty of activities? Then look no further than this stunning estate in Arrington.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Discover stunning National Trust site with 'something for everyone'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Love exploring National Trust sites and fancy a nice walk with plenty of activities? Then look no further than this stunning estate. Described as a "beautiful gem", families can't help but rave about the historic Wimpole Estate, in Arrington, Cambridgeshire. Built on more than 2,000 years of history, it features everything from Iron Age roundhouses to vibrant walled gardens. At the heart of the estate is an impressive 17th-century mansion with intimate family rooms that contrast with "lavish Georgian interiors". Visitors can walk among rare-breed cattle through "grand avenues" before entering shaded woodland. The estate also has a second-hand bookshop filled with gifts, homeware, books, local produce and gardening accessories. There is also a seasonal selection of plants for sale in the courtyard. Meanwhile, the Old Rectory Café offers light lunches, homemade cakes and specials, using produce grown on site. And if this wasn't enough, each year the estate transforms into an illuminated festive trail. More than one million lights form part of dazzling display of festive magic, making it the perfect Christmas evening out. On TripAdvisor, the estate has more than 640 'excellent' reviews, with visitors recommending it as a must visit for families and nature lovers. Elsewhere, on Google Reviews, Wimpole Hall has a score of 4.6 out of 5 from more than 7,800 reviews. It should come as no surprise, then, it has received rave reviews over the years. Unsurprisingly, it has received a tidal wave of rave reviews of the years, with visitors praising it as a "great day out". One recent review read: "Something for all the family. Lots of walks. Historic and working farm with animals up close, lovely gardens and trees. "Places for picnics. The house is well worth taking time over. Volunteers eager to share their knowledge and make sure we didn't miss the most interesting bits. Could even keep children engaged." Another added: "Been going here for years and love it. Great day out. The farms is amazing for kids with an incredible playground. "Beautiful walks round the estate. The house is massive and the guides know their stuff and are always on hand to help out." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:

The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A huge storage and distribution development could be coming to the edge of a Huntingdonshire village if plans are approved. The 10 hectare site would sit on land north of Cambridge Road, in Fenstanton, which is comprised largely of agricultural fields. An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Scoping Report for the proposed development was submitted on September 2. It was lodged by Pegasus Group on behalf of the applicant Markham and George Property Limited. Plans comprise an outline planning application for up to 100,000 square metres of general industrial, storage and distribution floor space. Commercial, business, industrial, storage and distribution uses are also proposed as well as parking for both cars and HGVs. The development would feature sustainable transport networks for pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles. As part of this, the junction for London Road and St Ives road would be upgraded to a roundabout to provide access to the site. The new roundabout is "considered an improvement and a significant local benefit", the report said. Read more New 3G football pitch approved despite fears it would make noise problem worse
    Progress update on £329m A141 and St Ives transport scheme
    Hunts council motion to remove support from controversial car park plans
    Call for Huntingdonshire draft Local Plan decision to be delayed amid concerns
    Leading Hunts councillor details where our food waste goes after collection If approved, the development would provide "multiple socio-economic benefits to the existing communities." "Employment will be provided during the construction and operational phases of the proposed development," it added. A "limited number of people" are set to be affected by the proposal in areas relating to "visual amenity, vibration and transport". "The proposed development is permanent, but its operation will reflect the normal operation of a employment development," the report added. "It is not considered that people would be adversely significantly affected by the proposed development once operational." Parts of the site are at risk of surface water flooding which will be considered in the design of the proposed development. The report also warned of "some potential for localised noise generation and degradation of air quality", although this would be limited to the construction phase. Sources of noise could include movements of HGVs, loading and unloading activities and the operation of equipment, machinery and plant. Vehicle movements related to both the construction and operation of the development could also increase compared to "the baseline level". However, the report stressed vehicles will be routed via "major strategic routes as opposed to local roads". The report concluded the development's nature, size or location is "not likely to have significant effects on the environment" and does not require an EIA. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Innovation is key for businesses entering Clean & Green Awards 2027
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: It's time to get your submissions in for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, to be in with a chance of being recognised among our regions top sustainability champions. As local enterprises look for more efficient ways to operate in a sustainable way, and encourage others to do the same, the innovators and disruptors stand out for what can be achieved here and further afield. Both the Energy Innovation Award, sponsored by National Grid, and the Game Changer of the Year award aim to showcase these types of organisations and individuals. Here, we learn more about these two award categories. The Energy Innovation Award sponsored by National Grid, will recognise innovations that significantly enhance energy efficiency or reduce energy consumption. From businesses to local communities, there are countless people actively looking at their green credentials, and this award will celebrate those who are meeting their environmental commitments in a way that hasn’t been seen before. The category is open to any individual or organisation that can showcase an energy innovation that is both unique and groundbreaking. Specifically, the judges will be looking for entries that demonstrate a novel and scalable approach with measurable results in reducing environmental impact, while actively engaging key stakeholders. Entrants will be expected to demonstrate how their innovation can be scaled or applied across other industries or regions, thereby maximising its impact. They will also need to show how they have actively involved energy providers, consumers or other stakeholders in their innovation. Critically, anyone entering this category must be able to evidence a reduction in energy consumption or improved energy efficiency, demonstrating measurable outcomes. If you believe your energy innovation is worthy of recognition, submit your entry by midnight on November 8. Meet the Sponsor National Grid sits at the heart of Britain’s energy system. Its individual companies run the networks and infrastructure that connect millions ofpeople to the electricity they use every day. These businesses own and develop the high voltage electricity transmission network in England and Wales, and the electricity distribution network in the Midlands, South West England and South Wales. Operating separately, National Grid Ventures focuses on competitive markets, investing in energy projects, technologies and partnerships such as electricity interconnectors. National Grid brings energy to life, with an ambition to serve customers well, support the communities in which it operates, and make possible a clean, affordable and resilient energy network of the future. The Game Changer of the Year award recognises breakthrough innovations transforming sustainability through measurable environmental impact and the potential for wider adoption (Image: Getty Images) The Game Changer of the Year category celebrates organisations whose ideas are making a difference to sustainability. The award recognises disruptive innovations that are changing the way industries, businesses or communities tackle environmental challenges. Judges will be looking for projects, products or services that go beyond incremental improvements and demonstrate real transformation. Entries should show clear environmental benefits backed up by measurable results. The winner will need to demonstrate how its innovation has reduced emissions, improved efficiency, conserved resources or delivered other positive environmental outcomes. Judges want to see innovations that have the potential to be adopted more widely, either across sectors, regions or even internationally. Successful entries should demonstrate how they have worked with industry partners, public sector bodies, communities or other stakeholders to develop and implement their innovation. The category was won in 2026 by Dura Composites, a construction supplier based in Clacton-on-Sea, Essex. Over the past five years, it has reduced embodied carbon by up to 33% across its core glass reinforced polymer (GRP) products and launched the UK’s first mechanical GRP separation system. Criteria The judges will be looking for a truly disruptive innovation that has transformed the sustainability sector. The winning entry should demonstrate significant environmental benefits, scalability and the potential for widespread adoption. Submit your entries before the deadline on Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information about the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To read about all of the award categories, please click here.

Cambridgeshire Police said officers are at the scene of an "ongoing fatal collision" and confirmed a pedestrian was "struck by a vehicle". summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Arts programme returns to 23 Cambridgeshire libraries this autumn
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Library Presents arts programme returns to Cambridgeshire libraries this autumn. Running from October 16 to December 12, there will be live performances, creative workshops and family events at 23 libraries across the county. Residents curate every event, which ranges from music and theatre to comedy and arts activities, with subsidised tickets available. Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "I’m delighted to see the return of The Library Presents which makes high-quality arts and culture events accessible to people across Cambridgeshire through their local libraries at subsidised prices. "These events provide a safe space, a welcoming environment and a sense of community. "I encourage everyone to take a look at the wonderful new autumn and winter event programme to see which fantastic events will be taking place near you." The line-up includes Yiddish music from Klezmer Foygl, award-winning folk from The Bookshop Band and interactive family concerts such as Hat’s Off! It also features immersive digital art, comedy, dance and a sea-shanty singing session at March Library. History fans can hear stories about the women of the Special Operations Executive, while ghost-story workshops will be held in Wisbech and Soham. Hazel Edwards, South East area director at Arts Council England, said: "The Library Presents shows how creativity flourishes when it’s woven into everyday community spaces. "This season’s resident-led programme brings high-quality arts experiences to people of all ages, with a real commitment to inclusion and wellbeing. "And in this National Year of Reading, it’s fantastic to see libraries transformed into places where everyone feels welcome to explore, connect and be inspired." Tickets are on sale online, by phone and at participating libraries, or on the door if available. More information can be found at www.library.live/the-library-presents. Residents helped shape the season by choosing from more than 50 live shows, including music, poetry, dance, digital art and magic.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "truly spectacular" Victorian home in Huntingdon has been listed on the market for £2.25 million. Located on Thicket Road, the detached house offers six double bedrooms and is described by the listing as "truly spectacular" and "impressively presented". The property’s accommodation is spread over nearly 5,000 sq. ft. and includes four reception rooms and three bathrooms. According to the listing by Carter Jonas, the ground floor features an entrance hall, kitchen/breakfast room, sitting room, dining room, media room, and garden room, as well as a utility room and cloakroom. Impressive – The Victorian home boasts a striking exterior (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) The kitchen is fitted with a "bespoke contemporary kitchen with integrated appliances including an oven, microwave, hob and dishwasher". A central woodburning stove sits between the kitchen and dining areas. The sitting room has an open fireplace and floor-to-ceiling windows that look out on the rear gardens. The first floor includes three bedrooms, two bathrooms, and a cloakroom. Two bedrooms on this floor have fitted wardrobes. Contemporary – The bespoke kitchen features a central island (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) Elegant – Floor-to-ceiling windows fill the spacious sitting room with light (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) The principal bedroom has a dressing area, air conditioning and an en suite with a double-sized shower, bath, “vanity sink unit with stone worktops, WC and heated towel rail”. A further three bedrooms, additional fitted storage, dressing room, and another en-suite are found on the second floor. A detached annexe is included in the listing. This offers a kitchen, sitting room, bathroom, and a first-floor bedroom and dressing room. The listing says the annexe enjoys a courtyard garden "positioned just off the main driveway" and has its own heating system. Contemporary – The bespoke kitchen features a central island (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) Outside, the property is set within grounds measuring close to one acre, with electric timber gates opening to a gravel driveway, described as offering ample parking. There is a double garage and a detached garden studio with a natural stone paved terrace and a hot tub. The gardens are described as predominately lawned and include a paved terrace, mature shrubs, plants, trees, a stable block, and additional store sheds. Expansive – The property sits in grounds measuring close to one acre (Image: Zoopla / Carter Jonas) Permission granted by Zoopla.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Entries are open for the East Anglian Clean & Green Awards 2027, including the Educational Trailblazer Award, which is sponsored by East Coast Energy Training Academy. This category will recognise businesses that promote sustainability through education, training or communication. Rachel Bunn, director of the training academy, said she’d be looking for examples of “innovation, collaboration and partnership” to support the education or training of staff or the community. The winner of this award will be able to demonstrate engagement with their audience and the potential for scalability. Rachel Bunn, director of East Coast Energy Training Academy (Image: ECC) Miss Bunn will also be looking for measurable data on skills gained and the learning that has taken place. She said: “The trailblazer will have gone above and beyond the norm and be able to show this through KPIs, evaluation data or outcomes.” This award acknowledges the importance of skills and training in meeting the regional skills needs. “This can be linked to CSR [corporate social responsibility], ESG [environmental, social, and governance] as well as going above and beyond,” she added. “It will raise awareness of your great work to the wider community.” The award will also showcase the great practice of the winning organisation and how education and skills are at the heart of its work. Innovation also plays a key role. It’s something that Miss Bunn said is “at the heart of mixing up skills in the region”. “The ‘do different’ approach should be at the heart of the nomination,” she added. “With the ongoing changes within communities and business, it is vital that employers evolve and create new opportunities.” Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. To enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To find out more about all categories, please click here. East Coast Energy Training Academy is located at East Coast College’s Lowestoft campus. The academy offers a range of commercial training to support the energy and engineering sectors and more. The college facilities are world class and training includes a range of bespoke and qualification models to meet the training needs of the sector as well as those seeking new career opportunities. Courses can support local and international delegates to develop skills as well as competency in areas such as offshore, emergency response, maritime, health and safety, renewable energy, leadership and engineering. The centre also supports bespoke training for sectors to meet evolving training needs and works with employers on new training models such as skills bootcamps and targeted diplomas in the workplace. The judges in this category will be looking for programmes that effectively raise awareness and promote sustainability through education, training or communication. Innovation, engagement and measurable outcomes in knowledge or behaviour change will also be key judging factors. Entries should have the potential for wider reach and scalability.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An ex-Cambridgeshire police officer "put the public at risk" after driving a police vehicle under the influence of alcohol. An accelerated misconduct hearing was held on August 25 at Lysander House, in Bedfordshire, for the former PC Joseph Passby. It was alleged the officer was involved in a crash with a taxi while driving the unmarked vehicle on Trumpington Street, in Cambridge. The incident occurred while the officer was on duty working from Parkside Police Station on June 15. Colleagues attended the scene of the collision and conducted a roadside breath test, the hearing heard. The former officer, who did not attend the hearing, provided a roadside breath sample of 110ug of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath. Officers initially believed the reading may have been affected by a cough sweet and the use of a vape, according to evidence reviewed by the panel. A further breath test was conducted at the police station where Passby provided a further breath sample of 113ug of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath. He was arrested on suspicion of driving whilst of the prescribed alcohol limit and taken to Kempston Custody, in Bedfordshire. There he provided two evidential breath specimens reading 88 and 81 microgrammes of alcohol on 100 millilitres of breach. On June 15, Passby was charged with driving a motor vehicle while over the prescribed alcohol limit. He appeared guilty to the offence at Luton Magistrates' Court on July 20 and was sentenced to a 12-month driving disqualification. Passby was found to have breached the standards of discreditable conduct and fitness for duty, amounting to gross misconduct. The allegations were found proven "on the balance of probabilities" with the hearing concluding that had he not previously resigned, the ex-officer would have been dismissed. He will also be placed on the College of Policing's barred list. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: “Police officers are expected to uphold the law and the highest standards of behaviour. "By driving a police vehicle while on duty and under the influence of alcohol, former PC Passby put the public, colleagues and himself at risk. "His actions were wholly unacceptable and the outcome reflects the seriousness with which we treat conduct that undermines public trust and confidence in policing." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: District council to move forward with local plan despite calls to pause it
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. More than 27,000 more homes could be built across the Huntingdonshire district as the area faces an ‘unavoidable reality’. Huntingdonshire District Council has approved the latest version of its local plan which highlights where more than 27,000 new homes could be built. The plan will apply until 2046 and was debated on Wednesday evening (September 9). Concerns were raised by residents and parish councillors that the number of new homes planned would essentially create a “new town” without the infrastructure. Under the local plan, more than 27,000 homes could be built in areas including Huntingdon and St Ives. Cllr David Keane said he had grown up in an estate built in the 1960s which had schools, doctors and dentists planned alongside it. The Conservative councillor said: “When I used to talk to older St Ives residents, they remember when all where I was living was fields. “Later I experienced a bit of that myself – the fields I knew disappeared and the landscape changed again. “Most of us don’t particularly like change, unless we’ve chosen it, but there’s one unavoidable reality – we do need homes.” He questioned whether this local plan was the right way to build new homes with infrastructure already strained. He said: “We cannot keep saying that the developer’s pound can be spent here, here and here – it can only be spent once to make this all work”. The plan would aim for 32,200 homes spread over 25 years, of which 4,400 are already built and 11,300 more have been given permission. Cllr Brett Mickelburgh told the council that 18 months ago, the government recognised Huntingdonshire as a “high growth area” and raised their housing target by 50 per cent. The Liberal Democrat councillor said this placed the council in “tilted balance” – where a housing shortfall weighs planning decisions in favour of developers. This means if the council rules against an application, it is more likely to be overruled by a planning inspector who could also order them to pay the developer’s appeal costs. He warned that this could lead to “speculative sites in the wrong places” and urged the council to support the local plan. Cllr Peter Gammons called the number of houses “outrageous” as it would be a 33 per cent increase compared to a national average of between 22 and 25 per cent. The Reform councillor said: “It would be a betrayal of the residents who voted for us and are already angry at the disappearing of their communities.” Cllr Keane said they need confidence not just that infrastructure has been considered but that it can be “realistically delivered” along with the homes. Cllr Alex Bulat said that after some of the “basket-case situations” on the council over the last few months it was “really difficult to find the good will to support the administration on any particular item”. The Labour councillor said: “I understand why residents are opposed to having a lot more new houses and I cannot blame anyone who is rightly questioning this plan. “Especially when they do not see the improvements to infrastructure and local services matching the level of development we have had in our area. “However, it is also true that we haven’t been building enough for decades.” Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray said she believed the target set by the government was “absurdly inflated” but without a local plan the market would decide where homes are built. The Green councillor said the plan was their only safeguard to defend their area “from hostile national planning targets”. Cllr Sarah Conboy, leader of the council, said that voting to support the plan was “not an easy decision” but they were unable to guarantee infrastructure in it. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “We will need to work with government to secure the things that we need government to deliver that we cannot enshrine in a local plan. “If we could guarantee all of the infrastructure first we would do that, but we can’t. “What we will commit to alongside this, though, is lobbying at every opportunity and making the case for Huntingdonshire and what it needs as it continues to grow – now, and for the residents of the future, and that’s something we can promise.” Cllr Mickelburgh said he was “really worried” about hearing a “chicken and egg argument” around infrastructure. He said: “Nobody is going to build a ten million pound water treatment plant upgrade if they don’t know the demand is coming. “You won’t find anyone investing in infrastructure unless they know the demand is coming and the local plan is how they know the demand is coming.” The council voted in favour of the pre-submission with 25 votes for, 17 against and five abstentions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: First look inside East Cambridgeshire's new crematorium and bereavement centre
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The county's newest crematorium has officially opened its doors with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by nearly 200 guests. After nearly eight years, Lake View Bereavement Centre in Mepal is ready to serve East Cambridgeshire—and project leader Cllr Anna Bailey could not be prouder. At Thursday evening’s grand opening, opened by Julie Spence, the Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, Cllr Bailey beamed as she saw her vision become reality. "I think it is absolutely wonderful; it is so unique and offers a service to the people of East Cambridgeshire that they have so far been missing," said Cllr Bailey. Around 200 people watched as Mrs Julie Spence, Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, performed the ribbon-cutting to officially open the new Lake View Bereavement Centre at Mepal. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "In the past, if people wanted a cremation, they had to travel outside the district; now they have this wonderful, purpose-built facility, which belongs to the whole community." The £13 million facility stands on the former Mepal Outdoor Centre, which lay derelict for years before becoming a peaceful place for families to say goodbye. Cllr Bailey said some people opposed the project and wanted to save the outdoor centre, but added: "We tried so hard to keep the outdoor centre. We saved it twice, and both times it failed. It got to the stage where the buildings were unsafe and had to come down. "It was being targeted by anti-social behaviour, and we needed to do something with the site, which had been taken over by nature. The chapel in the new bereavement centre can host around 200 people, including standing room. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "In fact, the site has some significant wildlife and plants and is a recognised county nature reserve. We wanted to make use of that to provide an environmentally friendly bereavement centre that took advantage of the beautiful setting, and I think we have achieved that perfectly." Cllr Bailey said the £13 million project was funded by developer contributions, including Community Infrastructure Levy and Section 106 payments, rather than taxpayers. "It has not cost a single taxpayer's penny, and has not landed the council with a debt that needs servicing, and we are proud of that too," said Cllr Bailey. Snow Drop Lodge has a tranquil setting overlooking the water with a large wooden platform for visitors to view nature and the beautiful surroundings. (Image: Sarah Cliss) She said the facility would welcome visitors 365 days a year and generate income for years to come. "I think we have created something very special and unique, and I hope that people will use it and take advantage of this beautiful site - I am just so proud of what has been achieved, and I am grateful to everyone that has been involved in the project," she added. The site can host up to four one-hour funerals a day. There is a garden of remembrance where families can have a plaque to commemorate their loved ones. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "We wanted to ensure people have the time they need to say goodbye with dignity, and not feel pressured or rushed. That is why we will be holding no more than four funerals a day, and there will be an hour in between each one," said Ian Scott-Logan, crematorium and bereavement supervisor. The facility has an all-electric cremator designed to cut emissions. The building has a large multi-faith chapel with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking trees and water, with room for up to 200 people, including those standing. There is a wooden covered walk way where families can view floral tributes for their loved ones. (Image: Sarah Cliss) A smaller side chapel seats about a dozen people, alongside two family rooms and a small room for people attending funerals from custody. Outside, a covered wooden walkway overlooks the water and gives families a place to display flowers. The site also has a natural burial area that will remain a wildflower meadow, mowed only twice a year. The Snow Drop Lodge can be used by families to hold wakes after funerals, while it can also be used by the community for other small events. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The site also has a pet cemetery for animals from hamsters to horses, but the centre does not offer pet cremations. Families can install remembrance plaques in the memorial garden, beyond which stands Snowdrop Lodge. Snowdrop Lodge is available for funeral wakes and community events. There is a wildflower meadow for natural burials. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Beside the water, Snowdrop Lodge has a large wooden jetty overlooking the site and will host a free bereavement café on the last Saturday of each month at 10.30am; booking is required. Mrs Spence said: "It is a privilege to officially open Lake View Bereavement Centre. "The care and thought that has gone into the design of this beautiful setting is evident throughout. It offers families a peaceful and supportive environment at a time when compassion, dignity and understanding matter most. The grounds are extensive and beautifully set out for visitors to enjoy. (Image: Sarah Cliss) "The centre will undoubtedly become an important place for local communities, not only to remember loved ones but also to find comfort, connection and reflection in its remarkable natural surroundings." Mrs Julie Spence, Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, gave a speech praising the new facility. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Around 200 people attended the official opening of the new Lake View Bereavement Centre at Mepal on Thursday evening. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Mark Whitten is the crematorium's technician and is in charge of the state-of-the-art electric cremator. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Snow Drop Lodge has a tranquil setting overlooking the water with a large wooden platform for visitors to view nature and the beautiful surroundings. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Mrs Julie Spence, Lord Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, performed the ribbon-cutting with the help of Cllr Anna Bailey, to officially open the new Lake View Bereavement Centre at Mepal. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Cllr Bailey said: "Lake View belongs to the people of East Cambridgeshire. Whether someone is arranging a funeral, attending one of our bereavement cafés, walking through the memorial gardens or simply finding a moment of peace beside the lake, we hope this will become a valued community asset for generations to come."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: East of England Energy Ambassadors urged to enter awards
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The search is on for the region's leading energy champion as entries open for the East of England Energy Ambassador award at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. Sponsored by GENERATE, the category celebrates individuals and organisations making a measurable difference through energy innovation, sustainability and leadership, while helping to shape the region's journey towards a net zero future. Judges will be looking for inspiring ambassadors who are influencing others, promoting the sector's strengths and showcasing why the East of England is a powerhouse for energy investment and opportunity The East of England Energy Ambassador award is open to those across all sectors – from clean tech start-ups and large-scale energy providers to educators, engineers, farmers, and local authorities. The award recognises those demonstrating leadership and innovation within their organisation or community. Ian Pease, business development manager of GENERATE (Image: DEPARTURE LOUNGE MEDIA) Ian Pease, business development manager of award sponsor GENERATE, said the judges are looking for “a genuine ambassador for the East of England’s energy sector” who is steering it in a “positive direction”. “I’ve seen firsthand how the composition of the East of England’s energy sector is changing as it continues on its journey to a fully decarbonisation energy system,” he said. “Part of my job is to manage GENERATE, established by local authorities in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex to attract and support inward investment and business growth in the East of England’s energy sector.” Ian said a true energy ambassador will be a leading figure and role model: a person who consistently goes above and beyond. “We’re looking forward to seeing entries from people who are making a real difference and positive impact to the East of England’s energy sector – people who go out of their way to promote our region’s capabilities and opportunities and why the East is such a great place to do business. “Entering this award will raise awareness of the good work and causes you are supporting, whilst raising your own profile amongst the East of England’s vibrant energy community. “It will also help to reinforce the incredibly important role the East of England’s energy sector plays in both region’s economic well-being and the UK’s energy security and resilience,” Ian added. “Take time with your application and make sure you include all the good work you’re doing – and your plans for the future too.” Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. To enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To find out more about all categories, please click here. MEET THE SPONSOR GENERATE connects the East of England to global energy investors by showcasing its unique energy offer, its highly skilled energy supply chain, and its unrivalled centres of innovation, research and science. A partnership of local authorities, GENERATE’s mission is to attract energy-related investment to bring well-paid, highly skilled and sustainable job opportunities to local people and businesses. Since 2021, GENERATE has profiled the region’s investment opportunities, ports and energy supply chain capabilities to national and international audiences. It works to raise awareness of the key infrastructure projects it is developing to support this mission, generating leads and enquiries from supply chain businesses keen to become part of the East of England’s energy sector. AWARD CRITERIA This award recognises a local business or individual who is leading the way in energy innovation, sustainability and leadership, making a measurable difference in the journey toward a net zero future. Applicants should be able to demonstrate how they are influencing, educating or inspiring others to think differently about energy.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Boy's face 'covered in blood' after 'extremely distressing' dog attack in park
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A mother has recalled the harrowing moment her son's face was left "covered in blood" after a dog attack at a Fenland park. Police received a report of the "extremely distressing" attack in Wisbech Park, Lynn Road, Wisbech, at around 6pm on Wednesday (September 9). A 12-year-old boy was injured and taken to hospital for further treatment as officers continue to investigate the incident. Zaneta Kubow, from Wisbech, said her son, Alan, had cycled to the park with a friend to visit a youth club and "hadn't heard from him". "The next thing I know I've got his friend's mum knocking on the door with my son and his friend who went with him," she recalled. "His whole face was covered in blood, his eyebrows were red, so I went to the police and they told me to go straight to A&E." Alan was taken to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital, in King's Lynn, before visiting a plastic surgeon at Norfolk and Norwich Hospital. He received six stitches around his eyebrow and nose and is now under the care of a consultant amid fears the attack could have damaged his nasal bone. "This has been an extremely distressing experience for my son," Ms Kubow added. "He is now terrified and frightened following the attack, and it has understandably had a significant emotional impact on him. "My son is a very active and sporty child and football and boxing are a very important part of his normal life. "Before this incident, he regularly attended football activities at Peterborough United and also played football at Wisbech St Mary Football Club. Ms Kubow revealed that Alan is now no longer able to take part in these activities due to his injuries. "He has been advised to stop his boxing training for approximately three weeks, and he is also unable to participate normally in his football activities while he recovers," she said. "Being unable to attend his usual clubs and activities has therefore affected his normal routine, socialising and enjoyment of everyday life. "He has already been left frightened and traumatised by what happened, and having to stop the activities that he enjoys has made the situation even more difficult for him." Cambridgeshire Police confirmed it has raised a crime of "allowing a dog to be dangerously out of control injuring a person" A spokesperson for the force revealed no arrests have been made and an investigation is ongoing. Those with information or CCTV footage should use reference 35/69822/26 and report it to police online. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Family says autistic five-year-old is a 'forgotten child' without a school place
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The family of a five-year-old Huntingdon girl are demanding action after authorities failed to find her a school place. Poppy Carter-Till lives minutes from two special needs schools, Prestley Wood Academy in Alconbury and Spring Common in Huntingdon, but has waited nearly 70 weeks for Cambridgeshire County Council to find her a suitable place. Her parents say she has become a “forgotten child”, left without a special needs place despite countless emails, letters and help from a solicitor. Poppy, the youngest of Leisha and Daniel Till’s three children, is autistic and non-verbal and needs more support than a mainstream school can provide. Read more Cambridgeshire council calls on government to deliver promised special needs schools Green light for two new special schools with 270 places Council consult on plans for SEND provision for autistic pupils at school 86-year-old St Neots care home resident fulfils dream with first helicopter flight Woman arrested after 'distraction burglary' in Huntingdonshire town Leisha said the family had met every requirement for a place, but the council still had not found one for Poppy. "We have done everything we can to try to make the process as smooth as possible. We got Poppy an early diagnosis. We have got her an EHCP (Education, Health and Care Plan) in place after seeking a solicitor's help, but still Poppy has been left without a school to go to," said Leisha. Poppy could have started school last September, but her late-summer birthday and additional needs led the family to wait a year, Leisha said. "We kept Poppy back a year, so the council has had an extra year to get this sorted out, but they have failed to do anything," said Leisha. Poppy has been given 15 hours of education outside school, but the sessions are in Cambridge, and the family cannot get her there without neglecting the needs of their other two children, Leisha said. Poppy’s older brother Kai, 17, is autistic and lives in supported accommodation but still relies heavily on his parents. Their middle child, Evelyn, attends mainstream school. "I can't physically get Evelyn to school and be in Cambridge at the same time for Poppy. If I take Evelyn to school, then we will be more than an hour late for Poppy's sessions, which, when she only has 15 hours a week, makes it worthless," said Leisha, who is also balancing work around her children's needs. Leisha and Daniel have both taken jobs at Evelyn’s school to make family life easier, but their income has fallen as a result. Leisha said: "It is just so hard. Poppy is a bright, happy little girl who has so much potential, but she is being denied the chance to fulfil that because Cambridgeshire County Council has not found her a suitable school place. "We have been told that they have approached lots of different special needs schools, and all have said they don't have the capacity to take Poppy, but we have no idea which schools, or why they feel they can't have Poppy. "It is so frustrating; not one person has come out to meet Poppy in person. They are making decisions about a child they haven't even met, based on what's written about her. "If I were to take Poppy or the other children out of school for a holiday, I would be fined or find myself in court. Yet what repercussions are there for a local authority which is failing to provide a child with an education? "It seems there is one rule for them and another for us. Poppy deserves the chance to learn in an environment that is tailored to meet her needs. "We cannot continue to be left waiting without clear answers or meaningful action. Poppy has already been without the education and provision she is entitled to due to failings of the local authority, and we need certainty that we are shown the respect as Poppy’s parents who are fighting for her future that you will listen to us. "We know that Poppy is not alone and there are hundreds of other families in a similar situation to ours, which is why we are speaking out. It's not just to get action for Poppy, but it is to hopefully help stop other families going through what we are going through." A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “We are committed to delivering good quality and financially sustainable education placements for all children, including those with SEND, in education settings closer to home. “The continued increase in demands for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) over the last few years, in line with national trends, has led to significant pressure on in-county specialist placements creating uncertainty for families, like the Tills, and is driving up costs. “In some cases, we are still consulting with schools on the most appropriate placements for children for September 2026 entry. Unfortunately, these consultations cannot progress during school holidays, while schools are closed. “The council is working with the Department for Education to bring forward new in-county specialist provisions as soon as possible “We commission quality assured Alternative Provisions for students with EHCP’s that are unable to access mainstream education, while waiting for a suitable special school place to be allocated. Alternative provisions may include online and in-person learning, tutoring or therapeutic interventions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 high-rise buildings in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough still have unsafe cladding
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nearly 10 years on from the Grenfell Tower fire, ten high-rise buildings in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough still have unsafe cladding, but the combined authority say they are “confident” it will be removed in time to meet government targets. In a performance report given to the combined authority’s overview and scrutiny panel, it was noted that four residential buildings have had their cladding or flammable insulation partially or fully replaced. This included three high-rise buildings, of seven stories or more, and one medium-rise building defined as having five or six stories. This was the same number of buildings with unsafe cladding replaced as the last time the figures were brought to panel in June. The report noted that it is “ultimately the responsibility of building owners” to make sure that “risks have been identified and necessary action taken”. It said that “very good progress has been maintained” and the authority is “on track to carry out all necessary assessments and engagement with landlords” to meet their targets. Out of the region’s 34 high-rise residential buildings – 21 require no further action but ten still need to have their cladding replaced. Cllr Anna Bradnam, of South Cambridgeshire District Council, said she was “very glad to see” buildings assessed and fixed but “slightly concerned” that ten still hadn’t. The Liberal Democrat councillor asked what was being done to monitor them. Daniel Buckridge, performance and evaluation manager, said he had been advised that Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service had written to the owners “to check on their progress or what their plans are for remediation”. He said there had been an issue with the government sharing details of buildings that had joined the national cladding scheme, but when given access they would be able to “get progress updates on those directly from that system”. He said: “Once we have that, we’ll have a better understanding of what’s going to be delivered when and we’ll be able to then perhaps set targets for when we expect those remediations to be complete.” Cllr Bradnam said: “I don’t know how many years we are on now from Grenfell tower, but writing a letter to the landowners seems a relatively mild thing to be doing. This is something that, actually it was quite some time after that, but the requirement came in that unsafe cladding should be removed”. Mr Buckridge said the target for cladding to be removed is December 31, 2029 for high-rise buildings and December 31, 2031 for medium rise buildings. These deadlines were introduced in July 2025. Of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough’s 144 medium-rise residential buildings, 59 needed no further action and 84 must have their cladding replaced. He said: “We’re working with resources that have been passed on to us, but this wasn’t previously a duty for combined authorities. We are confident that we’re going to meet those targets.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans to ‘reimagine’ bus services across Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Changes to bus services across Cambridgeshire have been outlined with alterations to 31 services listed. A report outlined a number of changes to the public transport system, with some stops dropped off routes, timetables altered and other services added. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority’s transport committee met on Wednesday (September 9) to note changes to bus services. The committee was given a report titled “Bus Services Reimagined” detailing the proposed final changes across the region. They did not have the final say on the plans, but were instead asked to vote on whether to recommend their approval to the combined authority’s board. Cllr Lorna Dupré, representing Cambridgeshire County Council, said she was “grateful for the honesty in the title” as “for too many communities it means the replacement of bus services with imaginary ones”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said that cuts to services were made necessary by the mayor’s decision not to increase the mayoral precept and divert funds “to subsidise car parking”. Paul Bristow was elected mayor of the combined authority in 2025 under the pledge not to increase the mayoral precept and avoid significant borrowing during his term. A report on bus franchising, which was approved under the previous mayor, warned earlier this year that Cambridgeshire bus services could be cut by more than a third in the next decade without additional funding. The Conservative mayor also promised to introduce free parking at council-owned car parks, with £1.5m allocated in his budget over two years to bring the policy to Peterborough and Huntingdonshire. Cllr Dupré said if residents aren’t sure if the bus they want to take will still be running in six months, they will “stop even considering public transport as an option”. She highlighted “losses for people” in the report – noting the 65 service will no longer stop in Buckden to bring residents to their GP. She said the Tiger On Demand service, which can be booked to stop at specific bus stops, is being used to “fill in gaps”. Labour councillor Angus Ellis, representing Peterborough City Council, said: “This should be bus services reduced, rather than reimagined”. Cllr Tim Bick, representing Cambridge City Council, said the combined authority needs to work harder at encouraging bus usage before axing services for low use if they are “serious about reimagining bus services”. The Liberal Democrat councillor noted the T2 and T3 buses, designed to link the peripheries of Cambridge without going through the centre, both of which will be replaced. He said: “We’re going to have to try harder to change behaviour in order to get the usage for a service like that. “If we want to do bigger things – we need to stick with change and support it.” If approved by the combined authority’s board, in February 2027 the first stage of changes would be made to bus services. In Fenland, services 56 and T7 will be redesigned to “keep important links” with the report stating links between March and Wisbech “would improve” with earlier and later journeys and better weekend provision. Timetables for the services 46 and 50 could change, including connections through Chatteris and revised times for Wisbech villages. In Huntingdonshire, the T12 would be withdrawn with improvements made to the 301 service between St Ives, Earith and Somersham. The 65 service would no longer stop at Buckden and would serve St Neots Rail Station, extending from the Offords to Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives. In Cambridge, the 8 to Hilton would extend to St Ives and combine with the 69 to “offer more links to communities”. The T4 between Addenbrooke’s and Newmarket would see a timetable and route change in Cambridge and Little Wilbraham to “improve punctuality”. The next stage would happen in August 2027, with several existing services in South and East Cambridgeshire serving Haverhill and the Newmarket area replaced with new services 119, 120 and 121 to make the network simpler. The 26 towards Royston would be increased to an hourly service, no longer serving Foxton, and extending to Guilden Morden every two hours. In South Cambridgeshire, new 27, 27A and 27H services would be introduced to replace parts of the services 7A, 17, 114 and T3. The 75 would be improved to provide hourly links to Cambridge and the T5 would have reliability and coordination improvements, including new evening journeys. The T2 service will be replaced by a new route from Cambridge North to Darwin Green, Eddington and the east of Cambridge city centre. In Peterborough, services 60 and 61 would be merged and there would be “minor changes” to the timetables of services 62 and 63.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Award shines a light on sustainability strategies that deliver
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Businesses prioritising their environmental impact are encouraged to enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. The Sustainability Strategy Award recognises organisations that are turning sustainability ambitions into practical action, delivering measurable environmental benefits while creating a framework for long-term progress. Category sponsor Opergy believes the strongest strategies are those that can demonstrate not just vision, but delivery. Johnathan Reynolds, managing director of Opergy Group, will be looking for evidence that sustainability is embedded within a business. “We are likely to be most impressed by strategies that are ambitious but practical, rooted in evidence and clearly connected to the organisation’s core purpose,” he said. “The specific theme matters less than the quality of the strategy. We want to see clear baselines, prioritised actions, accountable leadership, realistic investment and measurable results – including honest recognition of trade-offs, constraints and what still needs to be done.” Johnathan Reynolds, managing director of Opergy Group (Image: Opergy) For Mr Reynolds, entering the category is also an opportunity for organisations to take stock of their achievements and assess the effectiveness of their sustainability efforts. “The process should help organisations bring together their evidence, test whether ambitions are matched by delivery and recognise the contribution of colleagues and partners,” he said. Stakeholder engagement will be another area of focus for the category judges. “Sustainability challenges rarely sit within the control of a single organisation,” said Mr Reynolds. “Evidence of meaningful collaboration therefore tells us that an entrant understands the system in which its strategy has to work.” The entry deadline for the Sustainability Strategy Award is midnight on Sunday, November 8. For more information about the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To read about all of the award categories, please click here. Opergy is a strategic advisory and delivery partner working across energy, infrastructure, sustainability and regional growth. From its headquarters in East Anglia and teams across the UK, the firm helps businesses, public bodies and major projects turn complex challenges into clear, deliverable strategies. Opergy’s work spans clean energy, infrastructure, skills, supply chains, investment, decarbonisation and place-based economic development. It combines evidence-led research, sector expertise and practical delivery support to help clients make better decisions, build stakeholder confidence and create measurable impact. The judges will be seeking a project or strategy that excels in reducing or offsetting carbon emissions. Innovation, measurable carbon reductions and the potential for the strategy to be scaled or replicated elsewhere will be key factors. Collaboration with stakeholders will strengthen the entry.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Primark shoppers set for major change as delivery plans revealed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Shoppers are celebrating as Primark is planning to launch home delivery in Great Britain for the first time. The high street giant has traditionally focused heavily on its huge network of physical stores, but that is now changing as it looks to expand its online offering. Primark's owner, Associated British Foods (ABF), has bought a new warehouse in Sheffield to support the move. However, shoppers will have to wait for now, as the company has not revealed exactly when home delivery will launch. ABF said the service would come “in the future”. The move comes as Primark continues to expand its click and collect service, allowing customers to browse and buy selected items online before collecting them from stores. The new home delivery service could give shoppers another way to get their Primark purchases without having to make a trip to the high street. ABF said Primark's UK business had continued to perform better than some of its other markets. Like-for-like sales across the retailer are expected to have fallen by 2.6% over the financial year, which ends on Saturday, compared with the previous year. The biggest weakness was in continental Europe, while UK sales are estimated to have edged up by 0.6%. Primark said sales got off to a strong start during the summer, but the prolonged hot weather affected demand for autumn clothing as shoppers delayed buying their new-season wardrobes. Trading has improved in recent weeks as temperatures have cooled, the company said. Recommended reading George Weston, chief executive of ABF, said: “Our priority focus areas, the UK and womenswear, continued to outperform our other markets and categories. “Primark has made significant progress in building its digital capabilities and will continue this through both growing click & collect and by offering home delivery in Great Britain in the future. “There is now an opportunity for incremental and profitable growth through this channel.”
