The annual Heritage Open Day, taking place at Alconbury Weald, will be held on Saturday, September 12, from midday to 5pm. This year’s event will shine a spotlight on Alconbury’s military past, featuring an exhibition of artefacts from its World War II and Cold War-era buildings. Natalie Leigh-Brown, senior community development lead at Alconbury Weald, said: "Alconbury Weald has an amazing heritage dating back to early Bronze Age settlers and it’s a privilege to be able to share some of it at our Heritage Open Days. Alconbury Weald celebrates rich heritage with community fun day (Image: TIM GEORGE) "This year, we’re focusing on its more recent military past and the role Alconbury Airfield played in World War II and the Cold War. "The Community Association’s Family Fun Day running alongside ensures a great mix of culture and entertainment for residents and visitors, with lots for all ages and interests to enjoy." A talk from the Airfield Research Group will take place at 3pm, and pre-booked tours of the Cold War Avionics Building are already fully booked. Heritage Open Day explores Alconbury Weald’s military past (Image: TIM GEORGE) One of the day’s highlights will be a Dakota flypast by the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, scheduled for the afternoon, weather permitting. The event is part of Heritage Open Days, England’s largest festival on history and culture. Alconbury Weald Community Association will also host a Family Fun Day alongside the heritage activities. History and family fun combine at Alconbury Weald (Image: TIM GEORGE) Visitors can enjoy food trucks, Pimms, scones, face painting, live music, and more. Entry to the event is free, and most activities are available on a drop-in basis. Residents are encouraged to walk or cycle, while visitors can use the AW1 or 904 bus services to The Boulevard stop. Free parking will be available behind The Incubators, with signage provided on the day.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Business leaders welcome government support for small firms
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire business leaders have welcomed a government commitment to helping small firms grow following talks with the Minister for Small Business and Enterprise. The Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce voiced its support following a recent meeting with Lord Leong CBE, Minister for Small Business and Enterprise. Charlotte Horobin, CEO of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "It was a real pleasure to meet Lord Leong and discuss how we can work together to unlock growth for small businesses across our region and beyond. "Small businesses are the backbone of our economy, and they need the right support, skills, connections and opportunities to realise their full potential." During the meeting, chamber representatives highlighted the ongoing challenges facing businesses in the region, including rising employment costs, tariffs, and economic uncertainty. The conversation focused on digital adoption, export growth, and the development of skills, jobs, and apprenticeships. Charlotte said: "There is a huge amount of ambition among businesses across Cambridgeshire, and we look forward to working with Lord Leong and the Government to ensure that ambition translates into investment, exports, innovation, jobs and apprenticeships." The chamber is already supporting businesses with initiatives such as its AI Academy, a trade mission to Azerbaijan, PROJECT Fairfax, and the Local Skills Improvement Plan. Charlotte also emphasised the value of the chamber’s Quarterly Economic Survey (QES), which gathers business insights to inform national policy. She said: "Our Quarterly Economic Survey also gives us a powerful way to bring the voice of local businesses directly into the national conversation. "For us, that means our role goes beyond providing services to individual businesses. "We can take the collective voice of thousands of businesses and use it to inform policy and make the case for the conditions they need to grow." The chamber said it looks forward to welcoming Lord Leong to Cambridgeshire in the future and continuing its work with government and regional partners.

Commuters are being advised to allow at least an additional 60 minutes to complete journeys amid warnings trains may be delayed or revised. Disruption is expected until at least 10.30am, National Rail confirmed. A spokesperson said: "We have been advised of a swan on the track in the Peterborough area. "In addition, if the swan is found to be obstructing trains, services will need to stop on approach. This will lead to further delays. "Network Rail's response staff are attending as quickly as possible to make sure the swan is removed and the railway is as secure as possible." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Do not eat' warning issued to Tesco shoppers after 'health risk' recall
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tesco is warning shoppers not to eat one of its products which has been recalled due to a potential health risk. The supermarket giant is recalling the Tesco Finest Caesar & Smoked Bacon Coleslaw due to a packaging error. The mistake means that some packs may actually contain Tesco Finest Four Cheese Potato Salad, meaning that it also contains mustard not declared on the label. As a result, it is a possible health hazard for anyone with an allergy to mustard. Wednesday 3rd September - Tesco recalls Tesco Finest Caesar & Smoked Bacon Coleslaw because of undeclared mustard #FoodAllergy https://t.co/JRHL6RKA7q pic.twitter.com/YU0gMmSKs2 — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) September 3, 2026 The affected coleslaw comes in 270g packets and has a use by date of September 4. A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency said: “Tesco is recalling the above product from customers and has contacted the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. “The company has also issued a recall notice to its customers. These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. “If you have bought the above product and have an allergy to mustard do not eat it. Instead return it to any Tesco store for a full refund. “For further details, please visit the contact page of Tesco's website: tesco.com/help/contact.” Tesco added: “If you’ve bought the affected product and have an allergy to mustard, please don’t eat. “Instead, return the product to any Tesco store where a full refund will be given. No receipt is required. “No other Tesco products are affected by this recall. We’re sorry for any inconvenience caused.” If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: State Pension age rises to 67 - who will be hit hardest as age goes up?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of people are facing a longer wait for their State Pension, but some could be hit much harder than others. The State Pension age is rising from 66 to 67, with the change being phased in between April 2026 and April 2028. For someone who is healthy and able to remain in work, waiting longer may be manageable. But for others, those extra months could create a serious financial gap, particularly if they have little savings and are unable to continue working. A tax expert has warned that seven groups could be particularly vulnerable as the new State Pension age takes effect. The Work and Pensions Committee has previously warned that the impact of the increase is unlikely to be felt equally across the country. Andy Wood, a tax expert at Tax Barrister UK, said: “The increase means that affected individuals will have to wait longer before becoming eligible for their State Pension. “For those who are healthy, in secure employment and able to continue working, that additional wait may be manageable. "However, it could create a serious financial gap for people who cannot remain in work and do not have sufficient savings or other assets to support themselves.” The groups identified as particularly vulnerable include: These circumstances can overlap, potentially leaving some people facing several financial pressures at once. Someone who has spent years in a physically demanding, lower-paid job, for example, may also have caring responsibilities or health problems that make it difficult to work until their new State Pension age. Wood said: “These circumstances frequently overlap. Someone may have worked in a lower-paid or physically demanding job while also having caring responsibilities or experiencing health problems. “This can make it more difficult to build private pension savings, accumulate other assets or continue working until the new State Pension age. “People approaching retirement should therefore check their expected State Pension age and forecast rather than assuming they will automatically become eligible when they turn 66.” Recommended reading: The rise from 66 to 67 is not happening overnight. It is being introduced gradually, meaning the exact date someone becomes eligible depends on their date of birth. People born between 6 April 1960 and 5 March 1961 will reach State Pension age at 66 plus a specified number of months. For example, someone born on 31 July 1960 is expected to reach State Pension age at 66 years and four months. This means people approaching retirement should not simply assume that turning 66 means their State Pension will start. Wood said: “The exact date on which someone becomes eligible will depend on their date of birth. It is important to check this directly through the Government’s State Pension age service, particularly when making retirement or employment plans. “People should also check their National Insurance record and State Pension forecast. Reaching State Pension age does not necessarily mean everyone will receive the same amount, as entitlement will depend on an individual’s National Insurance history.” For someone unable to continue working, the wait for their State Pension could mean relying on other sources of income for longer. That could include working-age benefits or savings that had originally been earmarked for retirement. The Work and Pensions Committee has highlighted concerns about the potential impact on people who cannot remain in employment until their State Pension age. Previous evidence also indicated that when the State Pension age increased from 65 to 66, the absolute poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled. Wood said: “A delay of several months may sound relatively small, but it could represent a considerable loss of expected income for someone who has already left work. “Those without substantial savings may need to rely on Universal Credit or other available support until they qualify for their State Pension. Others could be forced to use retirement savings earlier than planned. “The change may be particularly difficult for people in physically demanding roles or those with medical conditions that limit the type or amount of work they can undertake.” The committee has called on the Government to consider increasing Universal Credit payments for 66-year-olds affected by the transition. The changes do not stop at 67. Under current legislation, the State Pension age is due to rise again from 67 to 68 between 2044 and 2046. However, that timetable could still change following future Government reviews. For anyone approaching retirement, the key point is that their State Pension age is determined by their date of birth, rather than simply reaching their 66th birthday. Checking the Government's State Pension age service, National Insurance record and State Pension forecast could help people understand when they are likely to qualify and how much they may receive. For those unable to continue working and without significant savings, knowing the date in advance could be particularly important when planning how to bridge the gap before State Pension payments begin.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare warbird forced to make a belly landing after engine issue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare warbird was forced to make a belly landing after suffering an engine issue during a maintenance check flight. The Fighter Collection's Curtiss P-40C Warhawk G-CIIO came down northwest of Royston on August 25 after taking off from IWM Duxford, in Cambridgeshire. The aircraft suffered an engine issue during a maintenance check flight which forced the pilot to perform a wheels up landing. The pilot evacuated unaided and directed the Duxford Fire & Rescue Team to the scene. The Fighter Collection said: "We are indebted to the IWM security team for providing mobile security units to the site ensuring the safety of the aircraft whilst the engineering team dismantled the aircraft." Highfield Farm staff helped lift the aircraft on to its landing gear before it was towed to safety. The Fighter Collection added: "We are further indebted to the Welch's Specialist Movements team who provided the logistics and highways permits to repatriate the airframe back to hangar T2S today." The Curtiss P-40C Warhawk served with several Allied air forces during the Second World War and was America’s third most-produced fighter of the conflict. The aircraft is rare in the UK, with G-CIIO one of only three airworthy examples before last week’s incident.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Miniature railway plans submitted for Huntingdonshire community nursery site
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A planning application has been lodged for a miniature railway at a Godmanchester Community Nursery after council enforcement officers halted work the project. The plan would put the railway along the eastern and northern edges of the five-acre, volunteer-run Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery on Park Lane, which includes a community orchard, with the aim of adding an attraction for families. A design, access, and heritage statement submitted alongside the application says work had begun on the railway track base before Huntingdonshire District Council enforcement officers stopped it, and the application seeks permission for the work already done and to finish the railway. Harry Quenault submitted the scheme for Godmanchester Town Council, with planning agent Chris McCrae acting for the applicant; the application describes it as the "installation of a miniature railway". Eye level image of the existing track installation adjacent to the southern 'platform 1', demonstrating its low impact on the land. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The statement says the railway would attract visitors while keeping rides affordable at £1, and supporters say it would offer families a cheap activity, encourage repeat visits and improve access to the site’s rare apple orchard. The design and heritage statement says the railway would complement, not replace, the nursery’s role as a community resource. It states: "The proposal is not to turn the site into a theme park. It is to add a modest attraction that complements horticulture, outdoor activity and community access." The document also points to Godmanchester’s railway heritage through the former Huntingdon to St Ives line, and planners say the attraction could introduce younger generations to the area’s railway history and draw more visitors. Eye level image traveling toward the northern end of the site, illustrating the track base prepared to receive the track prior to enforcement notice. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The railway would run mostly at ground level, with two platforms, a turntable at the northern end and a low timber fence around the track, and planning documents say the route is designed to minimise its impact on the orchard and neighbouring properties. The site is in a flood-risk area, but the applicant says the project qualifies as minor development and would not increase the risk, while the documents say the track would sit on maintained grassland and would not reduce biodiversity. If approved, the railway would run during fair-weather events only, from 10am to 3pm, Tuesday to Saturday. Aerial view of the site from the west looking towards the eastern boundary. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The design and access statement adds: "The purpose of the proposed Godmanchester Miniature Railway at the Community Plant Nursery is not simply to introduce a visitor attraction. It is to make an existing community-facing site work harder." Huntingdonshire District Council will decide the application later. Aerial view of the north-east corner of the site, and the relationship between the track and the eastern boundary and properties/community orchard beyond. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) At the nursery's Apple Day in October 2025, train rides provided by the Sawtry Miniature Railways Group doubled the team's previous daily record of 200 rides.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hacker used role at gaming giant to steal over £300k from players
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A hacker who used his role as a content developer at a Cambridgeshire company to steal more than £300,000 worth of "game wealth" has avoided prison. Andrew Lakeman, 32, formerly Jed Sanderson and known in gaming circles as “Mod Jed”, joined British gaming giant Jagex in November 2015. Cambridge-based Jagex is best known for its RuneScape games. In May 2018, Jagex’s player support team noticed suspicious account recovery activity with valuable in-game items, including gold, being taken. The activity stopped briefly so the team initially put it down to a glitch in the system, but it began happening again later that year. They realised the perpetrator was likely to be someone who worked for the company, as accounts were being recovered using information genuine owners would be unlikely to know. Jagex began its own internal investigation, which included creating a curfew for account recovery and modifying the firewall. It made these changes without informing the wider company so as not to alert the virtual thief. The sting worked and the Jagex IT department were able to identify Lakeman’s devices and home address as the source of the illicit activity. Jagex later sacked Lakeman and passed the investigation to Report Fraud, which referred it to Cambridgeshire Police in 2019. Officers found that Lakeman had sold the virtual gold and other valuable in-game items on the black market. Searches of his devices and accounts showed he had received more than £364,829 from cryptocurrency dealers. Messages to his wife showed he planned to make a fortune before leaving Jagex. He also discussed RuneScape accounts worth tens of thousands of pounds. Lakeman was arrested in July 2019 and charged with unauthorised computer access with intent to commit other offences, theft by employee, conceal / disguise / convert / transfer / remove criminal property and acquire criminal property. Lakeman, of Harbour Road, Beadnell, Chathill, Northumberland, later pleaded guilty to the offences and was handed a three-year sentence suspended for two years at Cambridge Crown Court yesterday (3 September). He was also ordered to complete 150 hours of unpaid work and a 25-day rehabilitation activity requirement. Additionally, a proceeds of crime act timetable, due to conclude in February next year, aims to recoup the money Lakeman earned from the thefts. Detective Constable Andrew McKeane, who investigated, said: "This was an incredibly complex and detailed investigation and certainly not one you see every day. "Lakeman was well aware what he was doing was wrong, and the hundreds of thousands of pounds he gained from selling the in-game items is no different to any other theft. "Just because it’s virtual, doesn’t’ mean he shouldn’t face the full force of the law. "I would like to thank my team for their hard work and diligence during what has been an unusual and lengthy investigation." "It is also important to recognise the significant assistance of senior Crown Prosecutor, Samantha Woolley, and Prosecution Counsel, Sarah Gaunt, for their drive and determination, which led to groundbreaking case law that was heard at the Court of Appeal. "Given the rapid growth of online and virtual worlds, the justice system is going to have to keep pace and adapt to these new and emerging crimes." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 86-year-old St Neots care home resident fulfils dream with first helicopter flight
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An 86-year-old care home resident from St Neots has taken to the skies for the first time. Eileen, who lives at Henbrook House, fulfilled her dream of flying in a helicopter after staff arranged the special trip from Bottisham Airfield Museum near Cambridge. Eileen and her daughter Fiona (Image: Henbrook House) She was joined for the experience by her daughter Fiona, taking in views of the Cambridgeshire countryside, including Ely and Newmarket. James Chandler, customer relationship manager at Henbrook House, said: "We were so happy to have been able to arrange this experience for Eileen and her daughter. Eileen enjoying the flight (Image: Henbrook House) "Trips like this obviously require careful judgement and planning, especially when health and mobility factors make accessibility tricky. "However, wherever it is safe to do so, we try to treat those barriers as problems to be solved rather than reasons not to try." Eileen, who once lived in Australia, often watched helicopters fly overhead and dreamed of seeing the world from above. The helicopter Eileen flew in (Image: Henbrook House) Although she encouraged her daughters to embrace adventure, her own reduced mobility in recent years made it difficult to join them. When staff at Henbrook House asked about an experience she would love to try, the helicopter flight quickly became the top choice. The care home team believes moving into residential care should not limit a person’s ambitions. Their philosophy centres on helping residents achieve long-held dreams and enjoy meaningful, personalised activities. This approach aligns with NICE guidance, which defines meaningful activity in care homes as physical, social or leisure activity tailored to an individual’s needs and preferences. Michael Zinaka, general manager at Henbrook House, said: "Our ambition is to challenge the idea that moving into residential care means stepping back from life. "Instead, a care home should be a secure base from which residents can keep enjoying familiar interests, spend time with their loved ones and try new things. Read more Miniature railway plans submitted for Huntingdonshire community nursery site NHS launches flu jab drive in Cambridgeshire and names who gets a free jab "Eileen’s experience is a wonderful reminder that later life can still be full of anticipation and excitement. "For us, exceptional care is about making those moments possible." Henbrook House, part of the Connaught Care Collection, opened in April 2024. It was named one of the top care homes in the East of England by carehome.co.uk in February 2026, marking its second consecutive year receiving the award.

Huntingdonshire District Council currently reports a housing land supply of 3.68 years, below the government’s requirement of five years. The applicant says the shortfall strengthens the case for small housing schemes. The land is currently in agricultural use and is screened from the road by mature trees and vegetation, with residential properties located to the north and west. The site lies adjacent to the Glatton Conservation Area and near White Roses, a Grade II-listed cottage dating from the early 17th century. The statement says the homes would have a "neutral impact" on nearby heritage assets because roadside trees would screen them from the conservation area and listed building. Historic England was consulted but declined to advise on the scheme. In a letter to the council, the organisation said its involvement "would not add value in this case" and recommended seeking input from the council’s own conservation and archaeological specialists. Permission in principle decides whether the site, its use and the scale of development are acceptable. If approved, a further application for technical details consent would be needed before construction could begin. The application is currently under consideration by Huntingdonshire District Council.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Throughout August, police received more than 400 calls about domestic abuse where they believed someone to be in immediate danger in Cambridgeshire. This equates to an average of 13 urgently graded calls about domestic abuse every single day. A spokesperson for the force said: 'Home is not a safe space for everyone, but we will always be here to help and will continue to work tirelessly to keep victims safe.' They are urging people to report any concerns to them, no matter how small or insignificant they may seem. Advice and support services are available on their domestic abuse web page.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: NHS launches flu jab drive in Cambridgeshire and names who gets a free jab
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough are being urged to get their flu vaccinations as the NHS begins its annual autumn programme ahead of winter. The NHS has begun its annual autumn flu vaccination programme in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, offering jabs to children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups. From September 1, vaccinations are available for pregnant women, children aged two and three (as of August 31, 2026), and children with certain long-term health conditions through their GP practice. Cali Makewell, strategic vaccination lead at NHS Central East, said: "Flu can be particularly serious for young children and pregnant women, which is why we're encouraging everyone who is eligible to come forward when invited. "Getting vaccinated during pregnancy helps protect both mother and baby, while children's flu vaccination helps protect them from serious illness and reduce the spread of flu to family members and others around them." Parents of school-aged children from Reception to Year 11 will also be asked to give consent for vaccinations delivered in most schools. Pregnant women can receive the vaccine through maternity services, GP practices, or participating community pharmacies. Last winter, more than 2.34 million people were vaccinated against flu across the East of England. The National Booking Service is now open for people aged 65 and over, those aged 18 to 65 with certain health conditions, care home residents, carers, close contacts of people with weakened immune systems, and frontline health and social care workers. Appointments for these groups are available from October 1 and can be booked online, through the NHS App, or by calling 119. Cali said: "If you're aged 65 or over, have a long-term health condition, are a carer, a frontline health or social care worker, or are otherwise eligible, you can book your appointment now. "Getting vaccinated ahead of winter helps protect you, your loved ones and our NHS services during what is often the busiest time of year."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Fifteen new police officers from backgrounds including tennis coaching, teaching and hospitality are set to begin serving communities across Cambridgeshire. The group was welcomed to Cambridgeshire Constabulary by Chief Constable Simon Megicks and will now be deployed to various stations across the county. The recruits, who are on the Police Constable Entry Programme (PCEP), will focus on police skills. The force is currently seeking more applicants for the PCEP, a two-year course with various assessments. More details can be found on their website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs man who filmed himself sexually assaulting sleeping woman jailed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man who filmed himself sexually assaulting a sleeping woman has been jailed. Kenan Samuel, 28, invited the victim and a male friend to his home in Alconbury Weald, near Huntingdon, for drinks on December 18, 2020. After the victim fell asleep, Samuel got into bed with her and touched her without consent. He filmed the assault while the victim was unconscious and unable to consent. Detective Constable Sally Muntane-Crane, who investigated the case, said: "Samuel is a dangerous man who took advantage of the victim when she was in a vulnerable state. Kenan Samuel "He was also cunning, deleting the evidence he had sent himself a nude photo from the victim’s phone without her consent." Police seized and examined Samuel’s phone after the victim reported the assault. Officers found he had sent himself a nude photograph from the victim’s phone, then deleted the message to cover his tracks. Samuel, of Lysons Close, was sentenced at Peterborough Crown Court on Friday, August 28, after admitting to assault by penetration, voyeurism, and causing a computer to perform a function to secure unauthorised access to data. He was jailed for five years. Det Con Muntane-Crane said: "I would like to praise the victim for reporting what happened, and for showing tremendous strength and bravery during the investigation. "I hope it gives confidence to other victims to come forward, knowing they will be listened to, and the police and wider criminal justice system will do everything they can to get justice for them." Further information and support concerning consent can be found on the police website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridge family issue Jeans for Genes plea after daughter diagnosed at six weeks
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge parents are urging people to support Jeans for Genes Week after their daughter was diagnosed with a rare genetic condition at six weeks old. Jordan Till and Drew Hanley are urging people to get involved after their daughter Halli-Ann was diagnosed with Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome. The rare condition affects around 500 people worldwide, including about 40 in the UK. Halli was diagnosed at six weeks after low muscle tone, feeding difficulties and periods of low oxygen sent her to neonatal intensive care. The Jeans for Genes-funded charity Unique helped Halli’s parents connect with families facing similar challenges. They are sharing Halli’s story to get people in Cambridge involved in Jeans for Genes Week, from September 14 to 20. Schools, workplaces and communities are being asked to wear jeans and donate to support children with genetic conditions. The 2026 campaign also features The Traitors winner Stephen Libby and his partner Daniel Quirke, who designed the official Jeans for Genes T-shirt.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New fitness studio inspired by Florida wellness scene opens in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new fitness studio inspired by Florida’s wellness scene has opened in St Neots, offering Pilates, yoga and strength classes with a focus on building community. Flow State, located at Unit C, 3 Tebbutts Road, offers a range of classes including Reformer Pilates, mat Pilates, yoga, and strength classes. The studio was founded by Pilates instructor Rose Parker, who spent time living in Tampa, Florida, and was influenced by the popularity and community atmosphere of studios there. Ms Parker said: "Pilates is much more established in the US, and when I was living in Tampa I loved the quality of the studios there and the communities that grew around them. "I wanted to create that same feeling back home in St Neots and make Flow State somewhere people actually enjoy spending their time, rather than simply somewhere they come to exercise." After securing the Tebbutts Road premises, Ms Parker enlisted Sandell Group to design and deliver a 10-week interior transformation designed to put community at its heart. The 1,900 sq ft studio was completed just 10 weeks after Ms Parker signed the lease. She said: "When I first saw the finished studio, I genuinely couldn’t believe it was real. "It was exactly how I had imagined it, and it felt like everything had been thought of." The design includes inward-facing Pilates reformer machines to encourage interaction among class participants. Ms Parker said: "I’d love Flow State to help more people in St Neots discover movement they love and become a place where the community can get stronger, meet other people and, most importantly, find somewhere that feels happy and enjoyable." Nissar Khan, head of business development at Sandell Group, praised the collaborative process and the finished result. He said: "Seeing Rose’s reaction to the finished studio was fantastic for everyone involved in the project. "We’re really proud of what we have created together."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Recently refurbished village pub seeks new landlord
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A recently refurbished village pub in Yaxley is searching for a new landlord to take over the venue and expand its food and events offering. The Three Horseshoes in Yaxley, Cambridgeshire, is offering a fantastic opportunity for someone to take the reins of a recently refurbished venue with a loyal customer base and room to grow its food and events offering. Presented in excellent condition throughout, the pub features a main bar popular for televised sport, a second bar area, and a cosy restaurant space. Refurbished Yaxley pub seeks new landlord (Image: Three Horseshoes) Angus Carrington, regional manager at Stonegate Pub Partners, said: "The Three Horseshoes is a fantastic pub with a well-established customer base and a great reputation within the local community. "Following its recent refurbishment, it's in excellent condition and ready for the next publican to hit the ground running. Village pub offers opportunity for ambitious new operator (Image: Three Horseshoes) "There is a real opportunity here to build on what's already successful by developing the food offer, creating exciting events and making the most of the fantastic indoor and outdoor spaces. "For the right operator, this is a chance to take a great village pub and unlock its full potential." The site also includes a fully equipped commercial kitchen, providing the ideal foundation for an expanded food menu and a stronger dining trade. Outdoors, the pub boasts a large garden with a patio, lawn, and dedicated children’s play area, as well as a tarmacked car park and additional land suitable for events or overflow parking. Three Horseshoes searches for landlord to unlock potential (Image: Three Horseshoes) Stonegate Pub Partners is seeking a community-focused publican who can build on the pub’s success while introducing new ideas to attract even more guests. The opportunity comes with private two-bedroom accommodation, making it a strong prospect for a live-in operator. Located just five miles from Peterborough and close to the A1, Yaxley has seen significant growth in recent years and benefits from attractions including Peterborough Speedway, Peterborough FC, and Longthorpe Tower.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Convicted Cambs sex offender jailed after setting up secret accounts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A convicted Cambridgeshire sex offender has been jailed for hiding online accounts, including one on eBay, from police. Justin Noble, 42, of Peterborough, was jailed for one year and two months at Cambridge Crown Court on August 28 after admitting he breached sex offender notification requirements. He was jailed for six months in 2024 after breaching a similar order made in 2016. MOSOVO officers uncovered the latest breach during a routine visit to Noble’s home in January 2025, when they asked to see his phone. He was previously given a six-month jail term in 2024 They found several undisclosed accounts and email addresses, including one on eBay, which Noble was required to report to police. Detective Constable Claire Cummings said: "Sexual harm prevention orders and notification requirements are there to manage risk and safeguard the public. "Breaching them is a serious offence, and we will take robust action against anyone who fails to comply. "I would encourage anyone with concerns about someone’s behaviour, particularly where children may be at risk, to report it to us."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest into death of 'beloved' Cambs mother who died unexpectedly at home
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An inquest has been held after a "beloved" mother from Cambridgeshire who "touched the lives of many" died unexpectedly at home. Gemma Connor, 40, a mental health practitioner from Peterborough, died at her home on October 12, 2024. A fundraising campaign for Gemma’s funeral costs raised more than £5,000. The GoFundMe page reads: "Gemma helped so many people through her work and touched the lives of many personally too. "She will be incredibly missed and we want to give her a lovely send off." Gemma’s daughter Jasmine told the Nottingham Post her mother’s death was a complete shock and that she “lit up every room”. The inquest into her death was formally concluded on September 3, at Vantage House in Huntingdon. Area Coroner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Caroline Jones expressed "sincere apologies" to Gemma's family for the amount of time taken to conclude proceedings. The inquest heard from Gemma's GP, Dr Deepali Prakash, that she had a history of health conditions including acute pancreatitis, fatty liver condition and alcohol dependency. She had also been prescribed several medications. The inquest heard from dieticians who Gemma had spoken to in early 2024, who said she was seeking advice on unintentional weight loss and nausea. She was advised to aim for a high energy, high protein diet and avoid too much fat. Gemma had been supported by a drug and alcohol service for alcohol dependency but asked for her file to be closed in April 2024. The inquest heard that on October 11, 2024, Gemma went to bed at her home in Peterborough at around 11.30pm. About half an hour later, her partner woke to find her unresponsive and breathing shallowly before calling 999. He was advised to begin CPR and the emergency services arrived soon after. Paramedics used a defibrillator and attempted resuscitation but Gemma was in cardiac arrest and they could not revive her fully. Her death was confirmed at around 2am on October 12, 2024. The post-mortem found no alcohol in Gemma’s blood but detected prescribed medication, including morphine. All the medication was within therapeutic levels except morphine, which was at a high, possibly toxic level. But Coroner Jones said the level could not be confirmed as toxic because this often depends on an individual’s tolerance. Gemma's cause of death was labelled as 1a respiratory failure due to morphine toxicity with contributing conditions of chronic pancreatitis and liver disease. Coroner Caroline Jones said this was not the same as an overdose because Gemma’s health conditions may have changed how her body absorbed the medication. In her closing statement, Ms Jones said: “I would like to extend my condolences to you all and Gemma's wider family and friends for your loss.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon stalker jailed after 'campaign of harassment' against victim
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire stalker has been jailed after sending a woman more than 300 emails in a "campaign of harassment". Carl Ashton, 46, of Coach Mews, Somersham, near Huntingdon, began emailing the woman in July 2025. The emails soon became obsessive, despite her repeated requests for him to stop. Detective Constable Sarah Hurrell, who investigated the case, said: "Ashton’s ongoing campaign of harassment left the victim living in fear, and in a constant state of emotional distress. "Ashton was manipulative in his emails, and used emotionally abusive tactics to prey on the victim’s kindness, guilt-tripping her into thinking he would harm himself if she did not respond." Ashton sent more than 300 emails between July and August 2025, many threatening suicide or self-harm. He repeatedly told her she would leave his children without a father and referred to his own funeral, blaming her for refusing to contact him. Ashton sent more than 300 emails to the victim (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) His behaviour escalated on September 6, 2025, when he turned up uninvited at her home at 4am. He tried to open the front door, shouted through the letterbox, dropped his keys inside and partly climbed through a bathroom window. She called 999 and police arrested Ashton. On Friday, August 28, he was jailed for two years and eight months at Cambridge Crown Court after admitting stalking and breaching a non-molestation order. The order was made in December 2025, but he breached it on May 11, 2026, by posting about her on social media. DC Hurrell said: "This behaviour is completely unacceptable, and its impact on victims’ lives cannot be underestimated. "Stalking and harassment can, and does, have a devastating impact on victims, whose lives are overtaken by obsessive and unwanted behaviour."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ten people jailed across Cambridgeshire this month for crimes from rape to arson
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From arson at a council office and a high-speed police chase to domestic abuse, burglary, drug dealing and sexual offences, courts handed prison sentences to offenders from across Cambridgeshire during August. Here are 10 people jailed during the month. James Conroy, 43, of no fixed address but from the Ely area, was jailed for 22 years and five months after grooming, raping and threatening a teenage girl. Conroy was arrested in September last year after police received reports he had been grooming the victim. During a search of a Soham property, officers found evidence of drug use and belongings belonging to the girl. He was released on bail with conditions preventing him from contacting the victim or anyone under 18. A month later, officers learned he had raped her. Conroy was arrested again but continued to breach restrictions. Police found cocaine and cash in his car, while he sent abusive and threatening social-media messages to the victim, including threats towards people she knew and a threat involving a meat cleaver. He had already admitted two counts of possessing cocaine with intent to supply. Conroy was also given a restraining order, placed on the Sex Offenders Register and made subject to a Sexual Harm Prevention Order. Matthew Howson, 33, of Grosvenor Yard, Newmarket, was jailed for one year and 10 months after starting a fire in the lobby of Huntingdonshire District Council’s Pathfinder House in Huntingdon. Police said Howson poured lighter fluid onto the floor and set it alight with a match on April 14. He then produced a Stanley knife before leaving the building, with a member of the public extinguishing the fire. He was arrested shortly afterwards at the former fire station in Huntingdon. He admitted arson, possessing a knife in a public place and breaching a stalking protection order. Andrew Dunkley, 38, of Ellison Close, Cambridge, was jailed for 22 months after leading police on what was described as an “incredibly reckless” high-speed chase. Dunkley reached speeds of 80mph in a 40mph zone, went through a red light and attempted to reverse into a police car during the incident in Trumpington in May. He was also disqualified from driving for three years and 10 months after admitting dangerous driving, two counts of driving while disqualified and two counts of driving without insurance. Anthony Woodberry, 67, of Harvey Street, Eynesbury, St Neots, was jailed for two years and four months after sexually abusing a girl under 13. The child disclosed what had happened to her parents on the same day, who contacted police. Officers arrested Woodberry the following morning and seized electronic devices containing extreme pornography. He was found guilty of causing or inciting a girl under 13 to engage in sexual activity without penetration. Woodberry was also placed on the Sex Offenders Register for 10 years. Ashley Smith, 38, of Eastleigh Road, Eastfield, Peterborough, was jailed for two years after repeatedly harassing his former partner in breach of a restraining order. Smith made multiple calls from withheld numbers, threatened to kill any new partner and told the victim: “You’re dead tomorrow, you’ll die.” He admitted three counts of harassment in breach of a restraining order at Cambridge Crown Court. Callum Liddle, 38, of no fixed address but from the Peterborough area, was jailed for two years and seven months after a prolonged attack on his partner. The victim was pushed, pulled by her hair, thrown to the floor and kicked. Liddle also pinned her down, covered her nose and mouth and poured cider over her face as she struggled to breathe. He admitted intentional suffocation, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and assault by beating. A 10-year restraining order was imposed. Joe Ross, 36, of Hawkins Road, Cambridge, was jailed for 16 months after stealing around £29,000 worth of jewellery during a series of offences across Cambridgeshire. Ross broke into Chloe’s Jewellers in St Ives using a hammer to smash display cabinets. He also burgled Stow-cum-Quy Post Office, stole coffee from the Co-op in Burwell and attempted to break into Burwell Post Office. He admitted burglary, attempted burglary and shop theft, and was ordered to pay more than £32,000 compensation. Kieran Jackson, 27, of Main Street, Ely, was jailed for one year and two months after police found more than 4,000 indecent images of children on his devices. Jackson was identified after images were shared through an Instagram account in October 2024. Officers later traced the account to his home address and seized two devices. Of the images found, 985 were category A — the most serious category. Jackson admitted three counts of making indecent photographs of a child and was made subject to a 10-year Sexual Harm Prevention Order. Jason Baker, 36, of no fixed address but from Soham, was jailed for five years and nine months after breaching a Sexual Harm Prevention Order by repeatedly meeting two 15-year-old girls and offering them drugs. He admitted three breaches of the order, two counts of supplying class A drugs and making an indecent image of a child. Baker had previously been convicted of a sexual offence involving a girl under 13 and was already subject to restrictions designed to protect children. Michael Richardson, 49, of Money Bank, Wisbech, was jailed for seven years after sending sexual messages to an undercover officer he believed was a 12-year-old girl. Richardson used the Kik messaging app to request sexual images and urged the supposed child to carry out sexual acts. Officers arrested him at his home in March and found 48 indecent images of children on his phone. He admitted making indecent images of children and several attempted child sexual offences, including attempting to cause or incite a girl under 13 to engage in sexual activity.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New 'school - keep clear' markings 'rubbing salt into wound' says councillor
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Freshly painted 'School - Keep Clear' markings have appeared outside an empty field in a Huntingdonshire village. The markings have appeared in Sawtry outside the site of Saltbrook Primary Academy, a long-promised two-form-entry school. But the school has not yet received planning permission or been built. Cllr Simon Bywater, county councillor for Sawtry and Stilton, said: "There’s just one rather significant problem. School Keep Clear signs have appeared on a road in Sawtry outside an empty field where a primary school has been planned for years, but is yet to be built. "The school they are apparently there for hasn’t even got planning permission yet, let alone been built. "This is the same school that residents have been promised for years, and which formed part of the justification for the closure of Gidding School a number of years ago. "Yet here we are. "We’ve got the school road markings before we’ve got the school." School Keep Clear signs have appeared on a road in Sawtry outside an empty field where a primary school has been planned for years, but is yet to be built. Plans for the school date back to 2021, when outline permission was granted for a wider development in northern Sawtry. The plans included land reserved for a primary school. Cambridgeshire County Council has since submitted detailed plans for Saltbrook Primary Academy, to be built in two phases. The first phase includes a one-form-entry school for 210 pupils, an early-years facility and infrastructure for future expansion. It will eventually expand to two-form entry, with room for up to 420 pupils. Read more Cambs man who filmed himself sexually assaulting sleeping woman jailed Cambridgeshire ‘school streets’ could be enforced with cameras Woman sexually assaulted in Hunts village as police ramp up patrols The fascinating history of St Ives island's basket makers Vape related blazes cost Cambs fire service more than £850 in just three years Cllr Bywater raised the issue in a letter to senior county council officers and the chair of the children and young people's committee. He described the situation as "poorly coordinated" and said it had caused "considerable and understandable frustration among local residents." He also questioned the decision to paint a bus stop marking at the site when no bus service currently operates there. He said: "Given how long residents have waited for this much-promised school, the premature installation of these markings is rubbing salt into the wound. "It creates the impression that resources and attention are being directed towards road markings when they are urgently needed elsewhere, before the fundamental issues surrounding the school’s approval and delivery have been resolved." He demanded an explanation of why the markings were installed, who authorised the work and whether the bus stop would ever become operational. Meridian Trust will run the new school, which is intended to serve children from Sawtry's new housing developments. The school is expected to open initially to Reception applications only before expanding as its first intake moves through the years. The council says construction will be timed using pupil forecasts and ongoing monitoring of numbers in the area. The first phase is expected to be completed before the school is needed. The council, Department for Education and Meridian Trust will keep the opening date under review to meet community needs without undermining Sawtry's existing schools. He said: "For local residents who have waited patiently for this much-promised new school, I can completely understand why the irony of these markings has not gone unnoticed. "Perhaps the county council administration could apply the same urgency to actually delivering the school as it has to painting the road outside it." He called on the county council to issue a formal statement addressing residents' concerns. Mr Bywater also said MP Ben Obese-Jecty had been kept informed and had asked to be briefed as the situation developed. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “These school road markings have been installed prematurely in error by contractors working on behalf of the Glatton Road housing developer. “As a school is not yet operational at this location, we have asked the developer to remove these school markings as a priority and at their own expense.” The early years facility is planned to provide 52 places, subject to demand, while the school design includes roof-mounted solar panels, natural ventilation and reduced reliance on artificial lighting.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire ‘school streets’ could be enforced with cameras
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council is considering the use of cameras to enforce school streets. School streets restrict car movements at drop-off and pick-up times to reduce pollution and encourage walking and other active travel methods. Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways and transport committee was asked to approve a report detailing their approach to using cameras to enforce traffic rules. They were told that “initial planning work” has started on installing Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras to enforce turning restrictions on roads such as Downing Street. Council officers also said they had started looking into using the cameras to enforce school streets, but these would need further assessment before being approved. Cllr Darren Green, of Romsey, said he was “very, very happy” that the council was considering this. The Green councillor said: “We know already that school streets can be very fragile and rely on a lot of volunteer work and best practice would be to back this all up with a camera system. “I hope going forward, once this is in place, that we can prioritise using cameras on school streets.” Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of the committee, stressed that volunteers would still be important regardless of if the cameras had been installed. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “When the general public see that there are actually members of the community willing to stand up and man the school streets, and protect that school, it has a much better impact that having a no-name camera that feels a bit like it’s the state doing it, or the council doing it, when actually most school streets are really supported by the parents and those there. “I think wherever possible I would support the use of volunteers on school streets but I do know that is increasingly challenging in some places. “In some places unfortunately the level of harassment that is given to those school streets volunteers means the cameras might be a better approach.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Free blood pressure checks at Huntingdon surgery as part of national campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon residents are being offered free blood pressure checks at Priory Fields Surgery on September 8 as part of a national campaign to identify the potentially dangerous condition. Priory Fields Surgery in Huntingdon is supporting Know Your Numbers Week by offering a free, drop-in blood pressure session on Tuesday, September 8 from 12.30pm to 2pm. High blood pressure, which affects around 14.4 million adults in England, is often undiagnosed and can lead to serious health problems. Dr Chris Smith from Priory Fields Surgery said: "High blood pressure is often called a silent risk because it rarely comes with obvious symptoms or warning signs. "However, leaving it unchecked over time significantly increases your risk of experiencing a stroke or heart attack later in life, and it can also quietly damage your kidneys. "The good news is that checking your numbers is quick, simple and straightforward. "Taking a few moments to get it checked gives you a clear picture of where you stand, helping you protect your long-term health before any harm is done." An estimated 5.5 million people are living with undiagnosed high blood pressure in England. The surgery, located on Nursery Road, is also encouraging residents to register with a GP if they have not already done so. Registration is available online at prioryfieldssurgery.nhs.uk/practice-information/new-patients.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We tried popular Hunts Chinese restaurant and it brought so much flavour
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire food reviewer Lucy Melton shares her thoughts following a recent visit to a popular Chinese restaurant in St Ives At the weekend I did something I haven’t done in years – went to a Chinese restaurant! Don’t get me wrong, I’ll have a takeaway every now and then, but it’s been years since I actually went to a restaurant and I’d forgotten how good it can be. We headed to The Welcome in St Ives, which has been around for years and has always had a good reputation. We decided to go for the à la carte menu over the buffet and it actually worked out cheaper. We had SO much food and even ended up taking some home. Selection of dishes (Image: Lucy Melton) I started with the chicken and sweetcorn soup, the thick broth and flavour were delicious, and it’s such a great way to start. We also had the chicken satay skewers, which were great, with loads of meat and plenty of flavour. Chicken Satay (Image: Lucy Melton) We had so much food but my highlights were the chicken in yellow bean sauce, a dish I hadn’t had before and I’m so glad I tried it. The Hong Kong style sweet & sour was really good too, it wasn’t too sickly, which I was thankful for, and it had crispy chicken, which is my favourite. The duck had amazing flavour, as did the shredded chilli beef, which had the perfect crunch to it. Shredded chilli beef (Image: Lucy Melton) The king prawn noodles were a massive portion as was the house special fried rice with garlic and soy sauce; you got so much meat, and both were great! King prawn noodles (Image: Lucy Melton) House fried rice (Image: Lucy Melton) The deep fried prawns were another highlight, big prawns inside, the batter was cooked really well and they came with a great sauce to dip them in. Honestly, I’d forgotten how much I enjoy sitting down and having a proper Chinese meal. So much food and loads of variety, I won't leave it as long next time!

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire bus services to change after combined authority review
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A number of bus services in Cambridgeshire are due to change following a review. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority (CPCA) carried out a review of bus services across the county to ensure the bus network was affordable, sustainable, evidence led and better aligned to passenger need. In Peterborough, the proposed changes include merging services 60 and 61, and introducing different timetables for services 60, 61, 62 and 63. They also include retaining the current loop around Werrington as part of the 62 service, helping residents to continue accessing Werrington centre. Service 60 runs between Peterborough Queensgate Bus Station and Orton Northgate, while 61 runs between Queensgate and Newark Sainsbury’s, 62 runs between Queensgate and Maxey, and 63 runs between Queensgate and Parnwell. A report to go before the CPCA transport committee on September 9 stated: “There would be no significant change to overall service levels [in Peterborough], but the network should be simpler to operate and explain.” The revised proposals were developed in response to a six-week public consultation that received 1,182 responses. Residents emphasised the need for reliability, punctuality, frequency, operating hours, access to rail and healthcare, the need for clear information, affordability and integrated ticketing, and the importance of services that were usable for work, education, healthcare, shopping and leisure. If approved at next week’s meeting, the changes could be introduced from February 2027, with further changes planned for August 2027. CPCA Mayor Paul Bristow said: “Thank you to everyone who took the time to share their views as part of our Bus Network Review. “Listening to residents is incredibly important, because you are the people who use these services and understand what works well and where improvements are needed.” Fenland – Services 46, 50, 56 and Tiger 7 would be redesigned to create a clearer local network, including improved March–Wisbech links, better weekend provision and revised connections through Chatteris. St Ives, Earith, Somersham and Ramsey –  The 301 would be improved to provide a simpler, more frequent core service, with Tiger 12 withdrawn alongside replacement links and implementation planning. St Neots, Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives – Service 65 would be revised to serve St Neots Rail Station and extend from the Offords to Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives. Cambridge and South Cambridgeshire – Services including 8, 26, 27, 27A, 27H, 75, T2, T4 and T5 would be revised to improve reliability, provide more regular Cambridge links and support evening, weekend and peak-time travel. East Cambridgeshire and Suffolk links –  Several existing low-frequency services around Haverhill and Newmarket would be replaced by simpler services, including new 119, 120 and 121 routes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
Share Share A Huntingdonshire school has apologised after children who opted for certain hairstyles risked being placed in isolation. Longsands Academy, in St Neots, told parents that students would be placed in "reset" if their haircut or hair colour was not deemed to be an acceptable style. According to the school's recently updated uniform policy, "harsh or dramatic contrast between the top of the hair and the sides" is banned. Patterns shaved into a scholar's hair or eyebrows, including an artificial parting, and "high or flamboyant hairstyles" are also outlawed. Meanwhile, skin fades where the pupil's hair is below a grade one and hair that is "teased, backcombed or covered in excessive product" are prohibited. For girls, hair "must be in a conventional and understated style" with hair clips or hair bands either "black or navy blue" in colour. Styles involving large bunches, buns or ponytails on top of the head "obscuring the views of pupils sitting behind" are banned. Under the rule, pupils would remain in isolation until parents grant permission for them to visit a hairdresser to have the hairstyle "rectified". The strict measure sparked a backlash among parents, with people describing the diktat as "concerning". Read more Cambs paedophile, 67, told young girl 'not to tell anyone' about sexual activity

They told The Hunts Post: "It is worrying that they are allowed to even suggest such requirements of students to all look a clone of one another and not celebrate difference. "The school has taken a significant directional shift since I was there. Focusing more on the policing of children than the teaching and ensuring learning is exciting. "With the booklet learning and scripted narrative, the policy around policing hair styles doesn’t surprise me - what does is the heavily racial focus of such a policy. "I think this policy, being so heavily drawn to focus on minorities could see for a significant rise in racial issues." "I find this concerning because it raises questions about how the policy was developed and whether the examples being used are fair and representative," they said. "Hair can have important cultural and ethnic significance, and policies concerning hairstyles need to be applied consistently and sensitively to all pupils." The parent added they have also sought clarification on how the police applied to pupils who are non-binary. A spokesperson for Astrea Academy Trust, which runs Longsands Academy, said: "We have recently updated our uniform policy to reduce the number of branded items students are required to have this academic year. "As part of this, we updated our haircut policy with illustrations to make clear the sorts of patterns that are not acceptable. “We have listened carefully to the views of parents who told us that these illustrations suggested that certain hairstyles such as cornrows were banned, which was not our intention. "We have worked closely with parents and carers and apologise that the policy was not clear." They added: "We will be sending out an update for families and students shortly. We would also like to thank parents who have contacted us and engaged so positively with us. “We are an inclusive school and we recognise and celebrate our staff and student identities from all backgrounds. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Job with The Co-operative Bank returned my confidence after Centerpoint support
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A young person who experienced homelessness says a job with The Co-operative Bank returned his ‘confidence’. Michael, spent most of his life in care. However, after he returned home from university his relationship broke down with his foster parents – forcing him into sofa surfing and eventually on to the streets. After a few months, he got in contact with Centrepoint, who were able to place him into accommodation and help him find a job. It was here that Michael started working at The Co-operative Bank, through it’s Brick by Brick scheme, and he hasn’t looked back since. He said: “Over two years I applied for 400 jobs. It was demoralising because I really wanted to work but couldn’t as employers would either say I was too experienced or not experienced enough. “Thankfully, Centrepoint and The Co-operative Bank were able to support me into this job now and I love it. Everyone’s friendly and supportive and it’s given me a purpose, as opposed to just existing.” Brick by Brick, launched earlier this year, is a pioneering early careers programme, designed to support young people into sustainable work and move on from homelessness for good. It provides a steady, structured journey starting with employability workshops, and then progressing to the Get Set Go Programme which provides six days classroom learning, mock interviews, professional behaviour guidance, and an introduction to the Bank’s values. After this, a young person will then complete work experience at the Bank which, if successful, is followed by an employment offer, removing the pressure of formal interviews. The program ends with an optional apprenticeship and keep in touch days, designed to improve preparedness between a job offer and start date. The initiative has had 35 young people participating in various steps so far with several securing permanent employment in the Bank’s Contact Centre. Michael is one of these, and discussing the skills it has given him, he said: “Communication, multitasking, timekeeping, but most importantly, confidence. “I’ve gone from thinking ‘Why would a company want me’ to now thinking ‘Why wouldn’t they’.” With over one million young people currently not in education or employment, Brick by Brick is reshaping conversations about homelessness by refusing to define young people by their experiences, instead investing in their potential and honouring their needs. “By meeting young people where they’re at, we can close the opportunity gap that holds too many back from reaching their potential,” said Anna Cuskin, the Bank’s Social Impact Lead. “Everyone deserves the chance to succeed. With the right support, young people can gain confidence, find meaningful employment and build a future beyond homelessness.” A man who was at risk of homelessness has told us how a new home gave him a ‘sense of purpose.’ Kai, 22, was living with his dad before overcrowding at home forced him to find somewhere else to live, he said: “It was a really worrying time. I didn’t know where to go or who to turn to.” Fortunately, Kai was able to get in contact with Centrepoint where through the Rent Deposits Scheme, funded by Nationwide Building Society, he was able to find a place in a House In Multiple Occupation (HMO). “It’s given me the stability to rebuild my life and slowly I'm getting back on track. “One day I'd like to live in a house of my own, by a river, on my own plot of land, and do what I want with it. “That’s my dream and I feel like if I keep sticking at it, I’ll be able to eventually achieve it.” However, young people in Kai’s situation may not be so fortunate – research by Centrepoint has found there has been a 10% fall in HMOs since 2019, with 458,000 in 24/25 compared to 510, 776 in 19/20. When asked if he had any advice for young people going through something similar, Kai said: “Don't give up. It might be hard, but right now, your best bet is to keep pushing forward and look for any form of help where you possibly can. Just keep going.” (Image: Centrepoint) The Prime Minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping has been given an early boost after the number of young people sleeping rough in London dropped by almost half. Between April and June 2026, 202 18–25-year-olds in London were recorded as sleeping rough. This was a 45% decrease from the same quarter last year when 368 young people were reported. The youth homelessness charity Centrepoint said this was cause for celebration and called the number proof that the Prime Minister’s pledge could be achieved. Lisa Doyle, the charity’s Head of Policy and Public Affairs, said: “London is providing the blueprint for what can be achieved when political leaders has the vision and intent to end street homelessness. “These figures are a real cause for celebration, but the job is not done. The Mayor of London and the Government must continue these efforts until rough sleeping is reduced to as close to zero as possible, and anyone forced onto the streets is helped off them quickly. However, the charity warned that ending street sleeping alone is not enough. “We must also remember that homelessness does not begin and end with rough sleeping.” Lisa said, “For every person on the streets, many thousands more are living in insecure or unsafe situations. To avoid reversing this positive trend, the Government must now also address the causes and consequences of those experiences too, and step up efforts to prevent homelessness.” A charity has warned that homeless people’s lives are ‘at risk’ due to the past few months of high temperatures. It comes after August saw another flurry of heatwaves – regularly rising over 30 degrees across the country. The UK’s leading youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint, believes council should do more to protect those sleeping rough when it’s this hot. Lisa Doyle, Head of Policy and Public Affairs, said: “This weather is life threatening for those forced to sleep on the streets. “And while many councils do activate protocols to protect those sleeping rough, there is no legal requirement for local authorities to provide shelter for everyone during severe weather. This must change.” “Ultimately, street homelessness is just the tip of the iceberg – the best way to keep people safe is to reduce homelessness however it is experienced.” Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The fascinating history of St Ives island's basket makers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share Keith Grimwade, Chair of the Friends group, describes the willow-weaving heritage of Holt Island Nature Reserve Osiers, the type of willow used for weaving, were grown on Holt Island from the 1720s to the 1920s. They give the island its name – ‘Holt’ is a local word for a plantation, especially an osier plantation. There was a big demand for willow wands (also known as ‘withies’ or ‘rods’) to make different types of baskets, and products such as filters for fire engine hoses and sieves for straining fruit in jam factories. In 1877 John Harrison founded ‘Harrison and Son, Willow Growers and Basket Makers of St Ives’. The firm prospered and became one of the largest growers of willow in the country. It had several osier plantations along the river, including Holt Island, and totalling 45 acres. Harrisons developed their own hybrid willow, ideal for basket work, a cross between Salix viminalis and Salix triandra. The willow wands were cut by men over the winter. In the spring the firm employed 70-80 women to remove the bark from the wands – ‘stripping the willow’, a call you may have heard when country dancing! From March to June men were employed to hoe between the lines of osiers. The willow wands on Holt Island were sorted, bundled and then taken by barge to The Quay, downstream of the town bridge. It was then transported by horse and cart to the Harrison’s workshop in Filbert’s Walk (now demolished). John’s son Charles, and then his grandson Jack, followed him into the business. One of their biggest contracts was making the sorting baskets for the Post Office. This was ‘square work’, which is much more difficult than making a round basket. The business closed in 1970, unable to compete with the introduction of plastic. But by then they had made over 30,000 potato baskets! Jack described basket making ‘as a work of art’. Fortunately, there are still people who have learnt, and pass on, this ancient skill. Join us on Holt Island on Heritage Open Day on Saturday, 12th September, when John Conkey of the British Basket Makers Association will be demonstrating traditional basket-making techniques from 10.30 am to 3 pm. There may be a chance for you to have a go at weaving, too. We will also have a display of Harrison baskets, kindly lent to us by Jack’s daughter, Charlotte. Share

These are the rules you should be aware of around licence plates from the DVLA. The number plates on your vehicle must: The characters must not be removable or reflective. The animal welfare charity revealed it receives a beating report every 15 minutes which represent a staggering 85 per cent of all its animal cruelty complaints. "It’s incredibly distressing to see such a massive rise in reports of intentional beatings with one report coming to our cruelty line every 15 minutes," RSPCA superintendent Jo Hirst said. "These are often upsetting cases where animals - usually pet cats and dogs - have experienced deliberate and horrific violence - leaving animals with not only physical injuries but mental scars as well." Nationally, the RSPCA received 16,033 reports of animal beats last year - almost double since 2021, when the figure stood at 8,459. Dogs and cats usually face the brunt of these attacks, but other animals are often victims too. And according to the charity, it is often someone in the pet’s own family perpetrating the violence. "To help rescue animals from these situations we rely on the public to be our eyes and ears and report any concerns about animal abuse to us and we are grateful that so many people do and are more aware of the problem,” Hirst added. "We’re also finding that CCTV footage, doorbell cameras and smartphones are providing a view into society that we never had before, meaning that animal beatings are more likely to be caught on camera in supermarket car parks, on streets, in lifts, and even behind closed doors in the home. "This could also account for the rise that we are seeing as they are more likely to be caught on camera, uploaded to social media or reported to us." Have you got a story you want to share?
