Citizens Advice Rural Cambs gives tips on how to deal with your debts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Meghan Hawthorne, debt caseworker at Citizens Advice Rural Cambs, talks about how debt and money problems in general can feel extremely overwhelming It is important to remember that you do not have to face this alone and we are there to support you. The biggest step forward is reaching out and asking for help. We know how nerve-wracking this can be, so in the case that you want to try and work things out yourself, or gather the relevant information before asking for debt advice, I wanted to give you some self-help tips on how to do this: Building your Budget: Knowing how much you have coming in and how much you have going out will show you how much money you have left over at the end of the month. · Start to gather bank statements, wage slips, benefit letters/information, etc. · You can build a budget sheet on paper, online or through a budgeting app. One we recommend is the online Money Helper Budget Planner: https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/everyday-money/budgeting/budget-planner Collecting Information on Your Debts: Knowing exactly what you owe to whom will show you your debt total and show you who you need to be contacting about your debts. · Gather statements, bills, contracts, letters, etc. Getting your credit reports (TransUnion, Experian and Equifax) will show you what money you have borrowed, paid back and owe. · Details to collect: o Who the creditor is (who you owe money to); o How much you owe; o What stage the debt is at (when did you miss the first payment and what has the creditor done to get the money back); o Your account/reference number. Contacting Creditors: It can be a good idea to contact your creditors, explain that you are trying to deal with the debt and ask them to: · Confirm the details of the debts. · Put a pause on chasing you until you have all your information gathered and work out what you need to do. · Stop adding interest and charges, which increase the debt. IMPORTANT: If you believe your debt(s) have surpassed the limitation period (6 years), please contact us before contacting your creditors. Priority and Non-Priority Debts: Priority debts have more serious consequences and can cause particularly serious problems if you do not do anything about them. · Priority Debts can include: rent and mortgage (or secured loan) arrears, council tax arrears, energy arrears, TV licence, court fines, etc. · Non-Priority Debts can include: credit cards, catalogues, unsecured (including payday) loans, unpaid water bills, money borrowed from family and friends, etc. When to Ask for Help: · If you are struggling to deal with your priority debts and/or you have more than one priority debt and don’t know which one to deal with first; · If you have completed your budget and don’t have money left over at the end of the month; · If you want to have a look at ways of potentially increasing your income and reducing your expenditure; · You have received court paperwork and/or have been contacted/visited by bailiffs. If you decide that you need to contact us for further support, our advisers will always be happy to help and guide you in taking the relevant next steps. You can contact us on Freephone 0808 278 7807: 9.30am-3.30pm Monday, Thursday, and Friday, and from 9.30am-7pm Tuesday and Wednesday, or head to our website https://www.citizensadviceruralcambs.org.uk/ for more information. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Urgent repairs needed at historic church threatened by water damage
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A council has agreed to help fund “urgent repairs” to a village church amid safety concerns. St Andrew’s Church in Wimpole had already spent £14,000 of their own money repairing the aging building from damage caused by water ingress and deteriorating masonry. The Grade II listed building is owned by the Diocese of Ely and, as well as providing church services, also hosts concerts, community events and art exhibitions. But the church’s future has been put at risk with water damage causing staining, plaster deterioration and even falling debris. The church applied for £2,000 of funding from South Cambridgeshire District Council’s community chest to continue repairs. This will also go towards restoring two historic monuments – reattaching the lion to the effigy of Thomas Chicheley and cleaning and refixing the brass plaque to Reginald York. The Church Is Located On The Wimpole Estate. Credit: Google Maps This will cost £3,719 while the roof and masonry work will cost £11,234. The church said they will meet their remaining costs through fundraising activities, existing reserves, private donations and applications to external funders. They have submitted applications to the Cambridge Historic Churches Trust and the Heritage Lottery Fund – and secured a £1,000 private donation, with indications of future private support. Council officers recommended approving the funding as it would support “the continued use of a well-used community facility and heritage site, ensuring it remains accessible to residents, visitors and researchers for years to come”. They said the repairs were necessary to stop the building deteriorating further and to improve public safety. The council approved the funding. Share

Unpaid carers invited to help shape future support services
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Unpaid carers in Cambridgeshire are being invited to help shape the future of support services. Cambridgeshire County Council is gathering insights from carers and those with lived experience of caring to help design future adult carer support services in the county. A series of workshops will be held between September 2026 and March 2027, offering carers a chance to influence service priorities, delivery models, and commissioning plans. Graham Wilson, chair of the council’s Adults and Health Committee, said: "Unpaid carers play a vital role in supporting loved ones and helping people live independently. "Their contribution is often unseen, but makes a huge difference to individuals, families and communities across Cambridgeshire. "We are committed to enabling full and healthy lives for all residents by helping to build strong community ties and supporting independent living. "That means listening to the people who use and rely on our services. "Carers understand better than anyone the challenges and opportunities that come with caring responsibilities, and their experiences are invaluable in helping us shape future support. "This is an opportunity for carers to have a real say in how services are developed. "I would encourage anyone with experience of caring to get involved and help us ensure support meets the needs of carers now and in the future." The first workshop will take place on Friday, September 18, from 10.30am to 12.30pm at Huntingdon Library. Attendees will discuss what future carer services should prioritise and the outcomes they want to see. This work also supports The Big Conversation on Care, which launched on 29 July and is the largest public conversation about adult social care in a generation. To take part or request more information, email Commissioning.FPTeam@cambridgeshire.gov.uk. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: World record attempt to test 100 men for prostate cancer in one day
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Eaton Socon Health Centre in St Neots will host an attempt to set a new world record on Saturday September 5. At least 100 men are expected to receive free prostate cancer tests and examinations in a single day. Miss Jyoti Shah MBE, a surgeon at North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust, said: "Prostate cancer is a silent killer, but it is a cancer that we can cure if we pick it up early enough. "It is the most common cancer in men in the UK, with one in eight being diagnosed as some point in their lives – and for men from an Afro-Caribbean heritage, the risk is one in four. "I am so very proud of and thankful to my team for their dedication and giving their time to support this important community event – and to our Hospitals' Charity for meeting the cost of the PSA tests." The event is supported by the St Neots Prostate Cancer Support Group and Purple Horizons, a community interest company based in St Neots. The current registered GuinnessWorld Records for men signing up for testing in eight hours is 258 in Egypt in 2024. Each PSA blood test costs around £3.50, with funding provided by the North West Anglia Hospitals’ Charity. Miss Shah and her team will register each patient on the hospital system, review medical histories, and carry out blood tests and physical examinations. All services are offered free of charge and on a voluntary basis. Patients will receive their results directly, and their GPs will also be notified. Further follow-up information will be provided as needed. The event aims to raise awareness of prostate cancer and encourage more men to get tested. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Amazing former Addenbrooke's Hospital patient Grace wins The Piano TV show
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A former Addenbrooke’s Hospital patient who lost her fingers and lower legs after contracting meningitis as a child has won Channel 4’s The Piano. Grace Matthews, 19, received a standing ovation after performing in the show’s final at Birmingham’s Symphony Hall. Pop singer Mika named her the winner after telling the audience that one performer had been able to “take the collective consciousness of thousands of strangers” and suspend it “in mid-air” through music. Grace, from Norfolk, said after hearing her name announced: “I’m shaking. I don’t know what to say. That’s insane. I did not think that would be the outcome at all, but thank you all, all, so much for coming and watching and thank you to the best contestants and partners I could ask for!” Grace Matthews, aged three (Image: CUH) Grace was three when she developed a temperature in January 2011 and was taken to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital before being transferred to Addenbrooke’s in Cambridge. Tests confirmed meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia. She spent nine days in intensive care and became critically ill, with surgery ultimately necessary to save her life. She lost all her fingers and both lower legs. Now using prosthetic legs, Grace plays the piano using her palm, half a thumb and the stub of a little finger. Her repertoire includes music by Pink, Adele, Queen and Bruce Springsteen, and she arranges the music herself.  Her mother, Vicky Matthews, said the family were “completely overwhelmed and incredibly proud”. She added: “To see how far she has come is something we will never take for granted. “We will always be grateful to the incredible team at Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals Foundation Trust and Addenbrooke’s who saved her life.” During Grace’s recovery, her former Addenbrooke’s music therapist Dawn Loombe and hospital play specialists became a central part of her day. Grace Matthews and her former Addenbrooke’s music therapist Dawn Loombe. (Image: CUH) Despite bandages on her hands, Grace enjoyed playing eight-octave rainbow bells while Ms Loombe played the accordion or guitar. After returning home to her parents, Vicky and Brian, and brother Tom, she progressed from a small electric keyboard to a full-sized electric piano. Ms Loombe supported Grace’s application for The Piano, and the teenager first appeared in the programme in June, performing Ludovico Einaudi’s contemporary classical piece Experience. Ms Loombe, now working part-time for Suffolk Music Therapy Services after retiring from Addenbrooke’s, said: “From the first time I met Grace, it was obvious that she was incredibly resilient and musically gifted. “She loved all the instruments, particularly the accordion, guitar, piano keyboard and the rainbow bells. She wanted to play everything and could copy melodies in no time.” Grace was selected for the final after performing in front of travellers at Birmingham New Street Station during filming for the series. Her winning performance at Symphony Hall moved the 2,000-strong audience, with viewers watching her receive the show’s top prize. You can listen to her music on Spotify. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Summer fitness tips to make exercise fun for the whole family
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Liam Rushmer, director of Cambridgeshire-based Fitness Rush Group, writes the first edition of his monthly fitness column Summer is a perfect reminder that exercise doesn't have to mean spending hours in a gym. Warmer weather naturally encourages us to venture outdoors, making it easier to move more without even realising it. With temperatures rising, it's important to train smarter, not harder. Stay hydrated throughout the day, wear lightweight clothing and, where possible, exercise during the cooler mornings or evenings. Your body works harder in hot weather, so listen to it and don't be afraid to slow the pace. The school holidays also create fantastic opportunities to build activity into family life. A walk along the beach, exploring a country park, swimming, cycling, paddleboarding, trampoline parks or simply playing games in the garden all count towards a healthier lifestyle. The best exercise is often the activity you enjoy enough to keep doing and are more likely to continue with it. Rather than focusing on calories burned, focus on creating memories. Children don't remember how many steps they walked, but they'll remember the adventures they had. Adults are no different. Aim to move every day, even if it's just a gentle walk after dinner or a family day exploring somewhere new. Every step contributes to your physical and mental wellbeing. As summer draws to a close, routines begin to return. Next month we'll look at how to build healthy habits that fit around busy work and school schedules, making exercise something that works with your lifestyle rather than against it. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Leading Hunts councillor details where our food waste goes after collection
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A leading Huntingdonshire councillor has moved to clear up confusion surrounding the disposal of the district's food waste. Residents had raised concerns about where food waste, which is now being collected by the district council, is sent for processing, with some believing it was being taken to the Envar site in Woodhurst. The confusion followed a recent site visit by MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who toured Envar to discuss operations and potential future plans, including a proposed medical waste incinerator. Councillor Julie Kerr, the council's executive councillor for parks and countryside, waste and street scene, posted on Facebook and said: "This is a clarification about HDC food waste service: Cllr Julie Kerr, who is the council's executive councillor for waste, has posted clarification on where food waste collected in the district ends up. (Image: Submitted) "There has been a lot of discussion following the recent visit to Envar by our MP Ben Obese-Jecty and some of the information subsequently shared on Facebook about where Huntingdonshire’s household food waste goes. "I think it is important that residents have the correct information." She explained that although Envar processes the district's green bin waste, food waste collected by Huntingdonshire District Council is managed through a separate system. This waste is sent to the Alconbury waste transfer station before being transported to an anaerobic digestion facility in March. Cllr Kerr said: "It is also important not to confuse the different waste streams. Read more Hunts district council asks for feedback on weekly food waste collections Fitness chain with 467 sites across the UK eyeing up 60 more new sites in 2026 Live updates as motorcyclist seriously injured in A14 crash Ex Cambs police officer accused of 'inappropriate' relationship with woman WATCH: Hammer-wielding thief caught on camera smashing his way into Cambs jewellers "HDC’s relationship with Envar relates to garden-waste disposal. "The food waste from Huntingdonshire is deposited at Alconbury waste transfer station, then it’s sent to the March Anaerobic Digestion plant for processing under the Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract that Cambridgeshire County Council has." At the March facility, food waste is processed to generate renewable energy and produce nutrient-rich material for use on farmland. Plastic bags are removed from the waste before processing. Cllr Kerr also addressed common questions about caddies and liners, noting that any type of liner can be used as long as it is not made of thick plastic. She said compostable bags are ideal, but bags such as bread plastic bags are also acceptable as long as bags used are not black plastic or bags for life. She encouraged residents to refer to the Huntingdonshire District Council website for official information. She said: "I appreciate that there are now a number of questions being asked by residents, and some of those questions are not currently covered on the website. "I have therefore asked officers to update the food waste information so that the additional questions being raised by residents are answered clearly and publicly. "I will also continue to make sure that residents have access to the information they need rather than having to rely on social media posts or assumptions about what happens to their waste." A food waste collections survey is currently open and will remain available until September 3. Cllr Kerr encouraged participation, describing it as an important opportunity to provide feedback on the service. During his visit to Envar, Mr Obese-Jecty discussed site operations and the proposed medical waste incinerator, which he opposes. The MP said: "I made it clear to Envar that I am against the plans to construct a medical waste incinerator and have been vocally against it since before I even became an MP, raising it with the Secretary of State, Angela Rayner, when she granted their appeal in 2024. "My thanks to Envar for taking the time to listen to my concerns and those of residents regarding the smell of the waste recycling process and the proposed plans for the medical waste incinerator." He asked people to let him know their concerns regarding the future construction of an incinerator at the site, and the impact it may have on them. He noted that a planning application for the incinerator has not yet been submitted. Envar’s next proposed development is an anaerobic digestion facility, with the incinerator potentially to follow. The MP also addressed complaints about odours from the site, especially during recent hot weather. He said there was no excess odour during his visit, despite high temperatures at the time. Share

Plans for a second 3G football pitch at One Leisure St Ives have been approved by Huntingdonshire District Council, despite concerns from nearby residents over noise. The council’s development management committee voted 11 in favour, with two abstentions, to approve the proposal at its recent meeting. The decision allows for a new artificial grass pitch at the California Road leisure site, alongside an existing 3G facility. The application was before the committee as the council itself, as owner and operator of One Leisure, was the applicant. A view from the south west corner of the One Leisure site. (Image: HDC) The development includes a 97m by 61m 3G artificial grass pitch, capable of accommodating adult 11-a-side football, nine-a-side, seven-a-side and five-a-side games. It will also include: The new pitch will be built south of the existing 3G pitch, on land currently used for cricket. Two replacement non-turf cricket pitches will be provided elsewhere within the wider leisure complex before construction starts. Two objections were received raising concerns that noise from the existing pitch would be made worse by the new facility. The existing 3G pitch. (Image: HDC) Councillors questioned whether the noise assessment accounted for both artificial pitches operating at the same time. Officers confirmed that it did, and said the council’s environmental health team had not objected. The report said general noise from the new pitch was expected to fall to around 46 decibels at the nearest properties, below the World Health Organisation’s 50-decibel guideline for garden areas. Intermittent sounds, such as whistles and shouting, were modelled at up to 62 decibels at the closest homes, but officers concluded this would not cause material harm when considered alongside the site’s established sports use and proposed mitigation. A plan showing the site layout. (Image: HDC) The pitch will be restricted to use between 8am and 10pm daily. Conditions will also require a noise management plan, a complaints and investigation process, and neoprene fittings designed to reduce the sound of balls striking the fencing. The proposed LED floodlights will be designed to direct light onto the pitch. Officers said replacing heads on the existing lighting columns would reduce edge light spill in some areas from about 46m to 18m, even with the additional pitch. Ecologists identified bats using the site for foraging and commuting, including light-sensitive species. Cllr Warren Smith front right chaired the meeting. (Image: HDC) Officers said the directional lighting and landscaping proposals would mitigate potential effects, while the development is expected to provide a 10.48% biodiversity net gain entirely on site. The plans retain 186 car parking spaces and 26 cycle spaces. A worst-case weekend-morning assessment estimated that the new pitch could require 96 spaces, leaving 90 available for the wider facility. The county highways authority did not object. St Ives Town Council supported the plans, while asking for consideration of parking and California Road maintenance. Sport England also raised no objection, subject to conditions on replacement cricket provision, pitch certification and long-term management. Before permission is formally issued, officers have been delegated authority to complete a detailed assessment against the National Planning Policy Framework, which was updated on the day of the meeting, and to add any necessary conditions. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thameslink's notorious 'ironing-board' seats set to be replaced
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Thameslink’s notorious 'ironing-board' seats are finally being scrapped after years of complaints from uncomfortable commuters. More than 60,000 seat base cushions will be replaced with upgraded versions featuring improved backrests, promising a more comfortable journey for passengers across one of the UK’s busiest rail networks. The upgrade comes less than 100 days after Thameslink’s operator, Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR), was brought into public ownership. Heidi Alexander, transport secretary, said: "This is what public ownership looks like in action. "Less than 100 days since GTR transferred into public control, we're delivering on the improvements commuters have been asking for. "From next year, we’ll start getting rid of the dreaded ‘ironing board seats’ so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes." First class seating will retain its current backrest design but will also receive improved seat base cushions. Seat back tables will be added to the 70 trains that do not currently have them. Transport secretary Heidi Alexander. (Image: Laurie Noble/UK Parliament/PA Wire) GTR says the upgrades will be rolled out over two years from next year, following extensive customer testing. Ms Alexander added: "We know fixing Britain's railway is more than a refurb job and moves like this are just the start of putting our railway back on the right track. "We've frozen fares for the first time in 30 years and publicly owned operators have added 76,000 extra seats on to the network. "Once established, Great British Railways will focus relentlessly on delivering a reliable, modern service that puts passenger experience at the heart of everything it does." This is one of several improvements planned by GTR following its move into public ownership in May 2026. Other changes include increased Gatwick Express services in December and an ongoing fleet-wide refresh of toilet facilities to remove graffiti. John Whitehurst, CEO at GTR, said: "Our customers tell us that comfort matters, which is why we've been working on plans to improve seating on Thameslink services and give the millions of people who use our extensive network a better experience. "Through customer research with everyday commuters, we've gathered valuable insight to help us shape the best possible solution for cushion comfort onboard our high-capacity trains. "We're pleased to move forward with plans and bring about those much-expected improvements." Share

The incident took place at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in the early hours of Easter Saturday, when Katie Good and her partner James Gingell from Peterborough arrived at the hospital as advised by the maternity team. However, before Katie could even make it across the car park, baby Oliver arrived unexpectedly. James said: "What followed happened incredibly quickly. "During the next contraction, Katie was standing holding on to me when her waters broke and in that same moment, our baby was born – so suddenly that he arrived into her clothing before we had fully grasped what was happening." Healthcare assistant Sam Craigie and interim deputy divisional nursing director Ana Jardim were nearby and rushed to help. Sam and Ana were nominated for an award for their quick thinking (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) Ana said: "When we arrived, things were moving very quickly and we had time to support the baby's head and helped mum onto the floor. "Both mum and dad were very emotional, and we were able to tell them it was a boy." The pair supported Katie safely to the ground and gently retrieved baby Oliver from her clothing, placing him on her chest in the moments before Emergency Department and Labour Ward staff arrived. Sam even took off his uniform to wrap baby Oliver in. The quick-acting duo were shortlisted in the Health Hero category at North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust's Outstanding Achievement Awards. The five were reunited at the ceremony, held at Peterborough Cathedral. Katie said: "It meant so much to us to meet the incredible people who helped us when Oliver made his surprise arrival in the hospital car park. Baby Oliver arrived before his mum Katie could even make it across the car park (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) "We've thought about them so often over the last few months, so having the opportunity to thank them in person was incredibly emotional and something we'll never forget. "It was also lovely to see their reaction to meeting Oliver all these months later – it really brought everything full circle. "It is a story we will tell for the rest of our lives, and one in which Trust staff will always be remembered with deep gratitude." James echoed her sentiments. He said: "In what could have been a moment of panic, Sam and Ana's composure and kindness brought an immediate sense of safety. “We are immensely grateful to every single person involved - from those who came running to help, to those who continued our care inside the hospital - in what was an unforgettable and dramatic start to Easter Saturday.” Share

The order had been issued on May 5 after Smith was convicted of stalking his former partner. Less than a month after the order was imposed, the victim discovered multiple missed calls from a withheld number, which she believed to be from Smith. He called again later that day and contacted a friend of the victim, who recorded the conversation. In the call, Smith asked about the victim’s whereabouts and whether she was with another man. He said that if she had a boyfriend, he would "kill him." Smith went on to make 22 more calls that afternoon, all of which were ignored, and the following month he continued to contact her from a withheld number. When she eventually answered, Smith threatened to come to her home and demanded to know who she was with. In a call the next day, Smith said: "You're dead tomorrow, you'll die. "I swear on my mother's life you're dead." Detective Constable Kyle Miskin, who investigated the case, said: "Smith’s behaviour left the victim living in fear and constantly looking over her shoulder. "Despite being made subject to a restraining order, he repeatedly ignored the conditions and continued to contact and threaten her." Smith was arrested at Stansted Airport on June 18. DC Miskin said: "Everyone has the right to feel safe following the end of a relationship. It is the third time in five years the estate has faced severe drought impacts and in response conservationists are accelerating a programme of climate adaptation. This includes tree planting, work to increase rainwater storage, and conservation grazing to reduce wildfire risk and support habitat restoration. The National Trust said selective breeding is also helping livestock cope better with dry conditions. Livestock have been forced onto winter feed months early (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) Dave Hassall, National Trust farm and countryside manager, said: “Drought affects every part of the system – crops, grassland, livestock, wildlife and costs. “We’re already using winter feed because summer growth simply hasn’t happened. “These pressures are being felt across all farming systems, and they show why adapting to a changing climate is essential for food production, nature and rural communities.” Parkland affected by drought at Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) The National Trust said Wimpole Estate is its largest organic in‑hand farm, with 1,200 hectares (3,000 acres) of land. Grain yields are down by around 25%, and straw production has fallen from 200 bales to just 60. Wildlife habitats are under pressure, with invasive species such as ragwort and thistles spreading rapidly in the dry conditions, and soil health has suffered with cracked ground. Veteran trees are showing signs of stress, and disrupted weather patterns are creating mismatches between flowering plants and pollinating insects – with consequences for both biodiversity and food production. It is the third time in five years that the estate has faced severe drought impacts (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) Efforts are under way to help the estate adapt in the face of climate change, with 125,000 trees planted since 2021 to improve shade, soil health, moisture retention and habitat resilience. The estate is trialling alternative forage sources such as willow and aspen, and exploring more drought-tolerant crop varieties. Mr Hassall said Wimpole Estate “has adapted for 2,000 years” and “that spirit continues”. In response, conservationists are accelerating a programme of climate adaptation (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) He added: “We welcome recent Government support for farmers, but long‑term resilience requires sustained investment in nature and climate adaptation. “We cannot do this alone.” The National Trust is calling on the Government to make climate resilience a national mission, led at Cabinet level, to invest in nature as essential infrastructure, and to support fire and rescue services. Members of the public can back this call by signing the trust’s petition at nationaltrust.org.uk/wildfire-petition. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts girl, eight, to swim five miles for terminally ill great grandma
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An eight year old girl from Huntingdonshire is set to swim five miles to raise money for her terminally ill great grandma. Isla, from Hartford near Huntingdon, is raising money for Brain Tumour Research by swimming five miles in honour of her much loved Great Nanny, who has been diagnosed with terminal glioblastoma. Glioblastoma are grade 4 brain tumours which are aggressive and often treated through chemotherapy, radiation therapy and surgery. The original challenge began as a two-mile swim, but Isla reached her £500 fundraising target so quickly that it was increased to £1,000. Isla's great grandma has been diagnosed with terminal glioblastoma (Image: Supplied) Encouraged by the response, Isla decided to increase her swim to five miles – the equivalent of around 322 lengths of a 25-metre pool. She will complete the challenge over several 500 metre sessions, aiming to complete the full five miles by September 26. Isla said: "I want to make Great Nanny proud and show her that even though I’m only eight, I can do something big for someone I love." As of August 23, Isla has completed 87 lengths, the equivalent to 1.35 miles. According to Isla's proud mum Freya, she has had amazing support from her family members who are cheering her on as she completes the swim. Isla’s fundraiser has already raised more than £800 and donations can be made through her JustGiving page. Isla is aiming to complete the full five miles by September 26 (Image: Francelli Photography) Her grandparents said they hope Isla’s story will inspire further support for Brain Tumour Research and raise awareness about brain tumours. They said: "We are incredibly proud of our granddaughter and her determination to do something so special for someone she loves." Brain tumours can affect anyone at any age and each year, nearly 13,000 people are diagnosed with a brain tumour. For more information, visit the Brain Tumour Research website. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Town ‘kept in dark’ over controversial car park plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A town council has accused a developer of leaving them in the dark over controversial proposals to build on a bus station and car park. Capital and Centric has proposed to turn Huntingdon bus station and Princes Street car park into 78 new homes and a “centralised hub” for businesses with green spaces. They have released similar proposals for St Neots and St Ives, sparking controversy across Huntingdonshire. Huntingdonshire District Council’s Liberal Democrat-led coalition even collapsed over the plans when two Green councillors left due to the council’s handling of the proposals. A special meeting of Huntingdon Town Council’s planning committee was held on Tuesday August 25 after the developer held their first public consultations last week and residents shared their concerns. Pam Hunt said she thought the plans were “unacceptable” and Princes Street car park is very “well used”. Peter Snow said: “Capital and Centric are trying to propose taking things away from the community but I don’t see what they are trying to give back – that’s why they are getting a lot of bad feelings.” He asked how much research the firm had done to suggest taking away a “well-used” car park. Angela Makey, owner of Niche Comic Book Shop, raised concerns over the impact of the loss of so many parking spaces. She said: “At the moment we’re a very short walk from Princes Street car park and losing a lot of those parking spaces will have a huge impact, not just on us. “We have a sustainable model because we’ve been going for such a long time, no new business will have that level of loyalty.” Guy Makey said that a lot of acts use the car park for carrying equipment to the Commemoration Hall and, without it, they could “simply move to a different venue”. He said: “As mentioned earlier, we lost Shakespeare at the George – which was very much the jewel in the crown of Huntingdon. It would be heart-breaking if the same happened to the Commemoration Hall.” Concerns were also raised about the proposal’s impact on the Cromwell Museum – both for those driving and those travelling by bus. Councillor David Landon Cole, chair of the planning committee, said: “I wish it was in our power to make a decision on this – it isn’t – but we do hear you.” The town council can only advise on planning applications, which are decided at the district level. A formal application to the district council has not yet been made. Cllr Phil Pearce said it was an “absolute disgrace” they were not made aware of the plans while six members of Huntingdonshire District Council sat on the town council. He said: “We hear your objections, we have the same concerns as yourself – we have been kept in the dark as much as you have. “There are other sites in Huntingdon which haven’t been considered and I think us as taxpayers really ought to be asking for our money back. “We’ve been let down – we’ve been kept in the dark and treated like mushrooms.” Cllr Alan Brugnoli said that during the consultation in Market Square the developer said it was “just a proposal – something ethereal”. He said: “They have been given this money and produced nothing at the minute. “They want high end properties with what they consider no parking, I just disagree. “Anyone that can afford to commute to London and back again, first is not spending money in the local community, but also they are going to have a car.” Cllr Pearce said that the bus station plans did not have enough bus stops to replace those lost which shows “an absolute lack of research”. Questions were raised around the three bus stops proposed to replace the station, which currently has 10 bays, and the lack of consultation with bus operators. Cllr Landon Cole said: “I don’t understand how you can design a bus station without talking to the bus operator, it’s very weird.” Cllr Pearce said: “I think Capital and Centric have lost the trust of the public and it’s going to take a lot to get that back.” Cllr Landon Cole said: “The lack of communication between Capital and Centric, HDC and the public is a real problem. “We [Huntingdon Town Council] hope this doesn’t damage support for redevelopment, but understand if it has. “If Capital and Centric are to remain in Huntingdon, they have a lot of work to do to rebuild trust – they didn’t offer anything to the people of Huntingdon, but tried to take things away.” The council agreed to co-sign a letter with the Commemoration Hall objecting to the plans, agreeing with one already submitted by the Cromwell Museum. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Five-year-old Hunts girl 'lucky' to be alive after appointment spots tumour
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A five-year-old girl from St Neots was diagnosed with a brain tumour just 12 hours after an eye test led to an urgent referral to hospital. Phoebe Carpenter had been suffering from sickness and severe headaches for several months before her mother, Katie Nicholls, arranged an appointment at Specsavers in May. The optician contacted the family after the test and advised them to go straight to Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge. A CT scan later revealed that Phoebe had a brain tumour. Phoebe Carpenter pictured on her way to the operating theatre for surgery to remove a brain tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) Katie, 41, said: “On our way home from the appointment, the optician called to say that, after speaking to his senior, we should go straight to A and E at Addenbrooke’s Hospital. “I felt like we were probably wasting the hospital’s time because Phoebe was running around playing like normal but, looking back, she was probably the sickest kid there.” Phoebe had previously been taken to a GP after months of symptoms. Katie said she was told her daughter may have migraines and was asked to keep a symptoms diary. After doctors carried out the CT scan, they told the family that Phoebe had a brain tumour. Phoebe Carpenter and her family pictured at Disneyland. (Image: Carpenter family) Katie said: “I fell apart and just sobbed and sobbed. I kept thinking, how am I going to tell her dad and the other children? “I kept asking if Phoebe would survive, but the doctors said they were unable to answer that at that time, which is the worst thing in the world as a parent.” Phoebe had a drain inserted to relieve pressure on her brain caused by hydrocephalus, a build-up of cerebrospinal fluid. The following day, she underwent a 10-hour operation in which surgeons removed most of the tumour. Phoebe Carpenter pictured after undergoing major brain surgery after being diagnosed with a tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) It was later confirmed as a pilocytic astrocytoma - a slow-growing brain tumour that usually affects children. Phoebe returned to school just three weeks after the operation, initially attending for a few hours before building up to full days. By the end of term, she had completed a full week. Katie said: “Phoebe is amazing. She went back to school three weeks after her operation. “She now wears glasses which are mega strong, but she’s very comfortable wearing them.” Phoebe Carpenter was left with a large scar after her operation. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe does not currently need chemotherapy or radiotherapy and remains under surveillance. Her first follow-up MRI scan is scheduled for November. Katie said: “Being told Phoebe had a brain tumour was the worst feeling in the world, but now we just feel so incredibly lucky because it could have been a whole different story. “If it’s just that she now has bad eyesight and wears glasses, then so be it. We are hopeful that this is the end of it, but we have seen just how quickly your life can change.” Katie completed Brain Tumour Research’s 88 Squats in July challenge to raise money and awareness after Phoebe’s treatment. Phoebe Carpenter pictured after her surgery and on the mend. (Image: Carpenter family) She said: “I just felt like I needed to do something to give back after the amazing care Phoebe received. We just feel so lucky. “Funding for research into brain tumours is so important because this really could happen to anyone. You never think something like this will happen to you, but it does.” Brain Tumour Research says brain tumours kill more children and adults under 40 than any other cancer, but just 1% of national cancer research spending has been allocated to the disease since records began in 2002. Phoebe Carpenter underwent major brain surgery after being diagnosed with a tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter underwent major brain surgery after being diagnosed with a tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter pictured with her older brothers. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter and her family pictured at Disneyland. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter and her older brothers. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter was able to return to school three weeks after her brain surgery. (Image: Carpenter family) Katie completed a gym challenge to raise awareness and funding for research into brain tumours. (Image: Carpenter family) Dr Noble added: “We’re incredibly grateful to Katie for raising vital awareness by sharing Phoebe’s story. The current funding for research is insufficient to deliver new, more effective treatments. That is why we are campaigning for governments to increase the national investment in research into brain tumours to at least £45 million per year."  Share

"A drier, brighter interlude may follow, but with a chance of further showers and thunderstorms breaking out during the afternoon. There is a small chance of sudden flooding affecting homes and businesses, potentially causing damage from floodwater, lightning, or hail. Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon, said in a previous social media post it was “alerted to reports that a child had allegedly been thrown into one of our crocodile enclosures” on June 18. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder following the incident and was later bailed as police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”. The suspect in the case reportedly has learning difficulties and had been on a trip with carers, and an investigation has been launched into his care. The boy sustained serious injuries after he ended up in the crocodile enclosure (Image: Newsquest) In an update shared on a GoFundMe page on Monday, the boy’s family said it was “nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home”. The fundraising page was set up to support the family financially and help the boy’s recovery and rehabilitation, which has raised more than £113,000 to date. “Now that we are home, our son’s rehabilitation journey continues and we can focus on ensuring our son has the best possible chance at recovery,” his parents said in an update posted on GoFundMe. “Both of us will continue to stay by our son’s side as we support him on his rehabilitation journey. “We attend the hospital frequently to find out the next steps and we work on them together as a family. The boy's family has since broken their silence on the incident (Image: Newsquest) “All of his immediate surgeries are over with for now, which means we can now focus on rehabilitation at home.” They said that the money donated so far “has supported us financially to cover immediate costs such as our bills and mortgage”, and “also allowed us to cover our loss of wages during this time”. They said they have bought and donated new toys to the paediatric intensive care unit at Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge and to the children’s play team on the ward. The boy was “very fond of the play team” and “they helped him be a little three-year-old boy by inventing new games and teaching him new ways to use his feet in play”, his parents said. The fundraiser for the toddler has raised over £100,000 (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) They said they had also donated to the Sick Children’s Trust charity, which helps support families whose children are long-term patients or in the paediatric intensive care unit. They also want to donate to the Addenbrooke’s Charitable Trust (ACT) to thank staff who were involved in their son’s care “including the supply of superhero costumes to brighten up his day”. Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said today that national resilience crews have been stood down after supporting the response to the blaze at Holme Fen for the past fortnight. Firefighters will remain at the nature reserve while clearance work continues and crews monitor for hotspots in the peat, which can continue burning underground. The service is reducing its presence to two crews during the day and one overnight, with the level of response to be reviewed daily. The national resilience crews were stood down at Holme Fen, marking a significant milestone in the incident. Chief Fire Officer Matthew Warren and Deputy Chief Fire Officer Jon Anderson met the firefighters at lunchtime to thank them personally for all their hard work in supporting our response. Mr Warren said the support from firefighters drafted in from other services across the country had been essential, both in tackling the fire and in keeping Cambridgeshire crews available for other emergencies. He said: “We couldn’t have dealt with this fire and made the progress we have without the support of the national resilience and neighbouring services’ crews. “Without their support over the last fortnight, we would have been left with very few crews to respond to other incidents, resulting in delayed response times, and the fire itself may have spread further into the nature reserve.” National resilience crews are firefighters from fire and rescue services around the country who volunteer to travel to other areas when additional support is needed. Mr Warren said some had spent days, and in some cases weeks, away from home while working in difficult conditions at Holme Fen. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man attacked estranged wife and son after demanding instant noodles
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A man who assaulted his estranged wife and son in an "abhorrent" attack has been jailed for more than four years. Tom Brown, 46, attacked the pair during a row that erupted over the absence of instant noodles at a home in Woodditton, near Newmarket, on January 4. Despite being separated from his wife, Brown was still living at her property at the time of the incident. The argument began in the kitchen before Brown left the house, returning about 30 minutes later. He became angry with his former partner when he discovered there were no instant noodles in the home. Their son and daughter tried to intervene, and Brown went upstairs, but he came back down shortly after and the confrontation escalated. The son helped his mother leave the kitchen, but Brown followed, tackled her to the ground, and pinned her down so she could not breathe. When the son tried to intervene, Brown pushed him to the floor, grabbed him by the throat, and strangled him for several seconds. The victims managed to escape and fled to a neighbour’s house. Brown followed them, shouting outside until police arrived and arrested him. Tom Brown attacked the pair in a row that erupted over the absence of instant noodles (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) He later tried to kick an officer in the head while being taken out of a police van at Parkside Police Station. DC Jack Sillince, who investigated the case, said: "Brown’s attack on his wife and son was abhorrent and he was incredibly hostile to police who came to intervene. "We wouldn’t have managed to secure this conviction without the support of the victims, and I’d particularly like to praise the son who protected his mum. "He was given a High Sheriff’s commendation and a £250 reward." Brown, of no fixed address, pleaded guilty at the start of his trial to two counts of actual bodily harm and one count of common assault of an emergency worker. He denied two counts of intentional strangulation which will remain on file. Brown was jailed for four years and eight months at Cambridge Crown Court on August 21 and handed a 15-year restraining order against the victims. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Motorcyclists in Huntingdon invited to apply for free training course
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A new road safety initiative is giving motorcyclists a chance to boost their skills. The scheme, aimed at improving rider confidence and safety, is open to those in Huntingdon and will take place in September. Peterborough & Cambridgeshire Advanced Motorcyclists (PECAM) has teamed up with The Huntingdon Freemen’s Trust and Cambridgeshire Police to offer 15 Huntingdon residents a free place on the RideSafe training day. Free motorcycle training offered to Huntingdon riders (Image: Supplied) A PECAM spokesperson said: "One of the things we really wanted to achieve with RideSafe was to remove some of the barriers to further motorcycle training. "You don’t need a big bike, you don’t need years of experience and you don’t need to be thinking about taking an advanced test. "If you legally ride a motorcycle and would like to become a safer, smoother and more confident rider, this day is for you. "Whether somebody has recently completed their CBT and rides a 125, has returned to motorcycling after many years away, or has been riding large motorcycles for decades, there is always something more we can learn." The event will take place in Huntingdon on Saturday, September 12, and is open to anyone with a CBT, A1, A2, or full Category A licence. The RideSafe programme is based on Roadcraft, the Police Rider’s Handbook, and the foundation of advanced riding schemes such as BikeSafe, IAM RoadSmart, and RoSPA. RideSafe scheme helps motorcyclists improve skills and safety (Image: Supplied) Participants will begin with a classroom session led by police motorcyclists and collision specialists, followed by practical slow-speed handling exercises. The day concludes with a one-to-one coached ride on public roads, delivered by a nationally qualified IAM RoadSmart motorcycle Observer from PECAM. The on-road coaching is tailored to each rider’s experience and needs. The scheme is funded by The Huntingdon Freemen’s Trust with additional support from Cambridgeshire Police and PECAM’s volunteer coaches. If successful, organisers hope to expand RideSafe to other areas across Cambridgeshire. Share

The meeting called for September 1 follows a request by Conservative group leader Cllr Ross Martin. It comes after the authority's two Green Party councillors withdrew from the council’s coalition administration, leaving it without a majority. Cllr Martin’s motion states that the council no longer has confidence in Lib-Dem leader Cllr Conboy as the council's leader and seeks her removal from office with immediate effect. The extraordinary meeting follows a developing political crisis at the district council, prompted by disputed proposals to build homes on car parks in Huntingdon, St Ives and St Neots - although the St Neots plans have since been pulled. Greens Cllr Stephen Ferguson and Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray announced in a statement last Monday (17) that they were leaving the coalition over the car park homes' plans, which meant the Liberal-Democrat administration no longer had a majority. Cllr Martin subsequently wrote to Cllr Ferguson calling for an extraordinary council meeting so members could vote on the no-confidence motion, and the date has now been set for next Tuesday when the motion will be the only item on the agenda. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: History looks at centuries of bad harvests in St Neots
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share St Neots historian Liz Davies shares a look-back on wheat harvest Bread has been a central part of our diet since the Neolithic period, over 6,000 years ago, when our hunter-gatherer ancestors began farming cereals and domesticating animals. Once people had begun to live on small farms growing cereal crops, the success of the wheat harvest, used to make bread, was of crucial importance, and across the centuries bad weather was feared because it could severely damage crops and lead to a poor harvest. A bad harvest would lead to less flour which would create bread shortages and also raise prices; and labouring families depended on bread for a large part of their diet. It was a run of poor harvests in the 1780s that sparked the French Revolution in 1789, when starving workers stormed the Bastille in Paris. The terrible weather continued into the 1790s and the failure of another harvest in 1794 led to food riots across England, including in St Neots in July 1795. By the Victorian period the successful ‘in-gathering’ of the harvest (as the St Neots Advertiser put it in 1866) was celebrated with church services, harvest suppers and local feast days. During Victorian times the Eynesbury Feast was always celebrated on the first Monday and Tuesday of September with toy and gingerbread stalls and ‘flying horses’ roundabouts on a field close to the village green. Hopefully, by the time you read this the drought of 2026, which has been the most severe drought in Britain for over 200 years, will be over. The last severe drought remembered in Britain was the drought of 1976 when locally, the hot dry weather led to hosepipe bans and water rationing and in some areas the only water available was from standpipes in the street. As the hot weather continued day after day students at Longsands School were allowed to wear their PE kit to school and the situation was so serious that the Government ran a campaign to encourage the public to use less water with its most memorable slogan being "Save water, bath with a friend". In late July the hot weather led to a plague of aphids on local farms and a company was called in to spray the crops with insecticide using a helicopter. Apart from insect problems many local farmers burnt the stubble left in their fields after the harvest and locally this started a serious fire on fields at Lower Wintringham Farm in July 1976. The fire began after a neighbouring farmer lost control of his burning stubble and set alight the unharvested wheat crop at the Wintringham farm, causing £3,000 of damage. Amazingly, the next day the same farmer himself needed the help of the fire brigade when his stubble burn again ran out of control. Drought problems continued until the end of August 1976 when Denis Howell, Minister for Sport was made the Minister for Drought but not long after that violent thunderstorms finally brought the drought to an end, although stubble burning was not banned until 1993. Whippet claims current proposals for Huntingdon do not include adequate facilities for bus passengers. This is espite supporting the wider scheme to deliver new homes and investment, a spokesperson said. The event, called Don’t Look Down, takes place on Saturday, September 19, during Blood Cancer Awareness Month and marks the charity’s 40th anniversary. Ms Mumford said: "When people think of cancer, they don't often picture a healthy 27-year-old mum with an eight-week-old baby in her arms – me included. "When I was sitting at the hospital during my tests, feeding my baby, I thought, 'They're making a big mistake here – I'm fine!' "Then the words 'you have cancer' brought a harsh ending to my naivety." Ms Mumford was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma shortly after the birth of her second child. This September marks six years since she went into remission. She said: "Through Lymphoma Action, I found the support I really needed. "They helped me understand what I was going through and connected me with others who understood – people who knew the fear of waiting for scan results, the grief of losing your old life, the uncertainty of not knowing what comes next, and the hope of life after treatment." Ms Mumford said she hopes to raise funds and awareness for those affected by lymphoma, the most common type of blood cancer in the UK. Laura Thompson, challenge events fundraiser at Lymphoma Action, said: "We are so grateful to Brittany and her family for their support. Four homes have been approved at a former kennels and cattery despite fears they could “open a floodgate” of development in the countryside. Plans for five houses at the site off Fenstanton Road near Hilton had been rejected in 2022 for being out of character for the countryside and being in an unsustainable location where residents would need to drive to access services. But the latest plans for four detached four-bedroom bungalows were recommended for approval by Huntingdonshire District Council’s planning officers. A design and access statement from Twenty Nine Architecture and Planning said the new plan “significantly reduced” the scale of the homes to a “modest single-storey form” more in line with the existing buildings on the site. The former Fields View Kennels and Cattery, which shut in 2020, would be demolished to make way for the homes. Hilton Parish Council still objected to the new plans and Cllr Peter Balicki spoke on its behalf to the council’s development management committee on Monday, August 17. He said that the last proposal was originally for seven homes before being revised down to six, and finally five. He said the parish council objected to these from “concern” that if homes were approved on the former agricultural site it would “open a floodgate of applications”. He said: “It just seems that you can turn the barrel of the kaleidoscope as many times as you like until it falls into place. “Now that we’ve gone from seven failed, six failed, five failed – we’ll let permission be given for four”. James Aldridge, of nearby Alpha Farms, said he was concerned that future residents of the homes could complain about his poultry farm – despite it being there first. He said: “Our farm is already here and is a working farm – there will naturally be noise, smells, dust, farm vehicles and muck movements. “If people move into these houses and then complain about these normal farming activities, could that lead to the council putting restrictions on our farm? “We want to know that our farm can continue to operate normally in the future.” The council’s planning officer said national planning policy states that existing sites “should not have unreasonable restrictions” placed on them as a result of new developments being approved nearby. An odour assessment also took place, which was not done for the previous application, and officers said they didn’t think odour or noise would negatively impact future residents. Cllr Alan Hunt, of St Neots Eatons, raised concerns that two parking spaces per home would not be enough and visitors would be forced to park on the road which could lead to a “real highway safety risk”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “From our visit to the site there was nowhere on the side of the road that I felt was actually safe for that kind of parking. “It’s a rural road, it’s a 60mph limit and the visibility is not brilliant.” Cllr Jon Neish said that even though cycle parking would be provided at the homes, they’ll still be largely car dependent as they would be “in the middle of nowhere”. The Conservative councillor said: “I wouldn’t want to cycle down there – I was lucky I was on a motorbike at the time, so it was two wheels, but it had an engine. “I just think it’s a little bit awkward myself and I’ve not been convinced that it actually is the right use for this.” Cllr Tom Sanderson said that, since the highway authority didn’t object to the plans, it would be “very difficult” for them to refuse based on parking or road safety concerns. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “If this went to appeal, the fact is we are in tilted balance – that dreaded phrase. “I think if this were to be rejected, it would be very difficult to justify doing so at appeal.” The application was passed by a single vote with five voting in favour, four against and four abstaining. Evri responds after delivery driver caught in Cambs with no insurance or licence
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Evri has responded after a delivery driver was caught in Cambridgeshire with no insurance or a valid driving licence. Police confirmed a delivery van with around 100 packages inside had been stopped by officers in St Neots on Wednesday (August 19). Cambridgeshire Constabulary said it would "have been a miracle" if the parcels had been delivered due to the "look of the van's tyres". In a statement, Evri revealed the driver was a third-party courier and added that the vehicle involved was not owned by the company. A spokesperson said it took safety and compliance "very seriously" and said it requires the same from its couriers. "We are aware of an incident involving a self-employed courier and his own vehicle, and we are investigating this with the individual in question," they added. "All of our couriers are responsible for ensuring that they have the correct documentation to provide service, including a driving licence and insurance." Evri said the vast majority of parcels handled by the firm are contracted to be delivered within five days. It confirmed the packages involved in the incident will be redelivered, with "the majority still delivered within the timeframe." Have you got a story you want to share? We tried the lunch menu at newly refurbished Prezzo Italian in Peterborough
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share I was very excited to be invited to Prezzo in Peterborough to try out their lunch menu after their recent refurbishment - and it did not disappoint. Firstly, the restaurant's decor is gorgeous. A member of staff told me they had undergone a complete revamp around six weeks ago to give the space a fresh feel, as before it was apparently a little dark. That certainly isn't a problem anymore; the space feels bright, airy and colourful with modern wood finishes and bold prints on the walls. Prezzo's interior (Image: Emily Stevens) Prezzo's bar (Image: Emily Stevens) My sister and I were seated near the front of the restaurant by the window, but the space is deceivingly large and extends back a long way. There is even a garden space at the back for outdoor dining. Prezzo's outdoor dining space (Image: Emily Stevens) We started off with drinks and both went for one of their homemade coolers. I tried the Wild Strawberry Lemonade, which was delicious, very refreshing and perfect for the unrelenting hot weather we have had this summer. My sister had a Citrus Cooler, which she loved as well and said it was very well presented. Wild Strawberry Lemonade and Citrus Cooler (Image: Emily Stevens) Next we shared the Tomato Bruschetta and some olives to start. We both agreed that the bruschetta was the highlight of the meal; the bread was perfectly crisp but still soft inside and the tomatoes on top were elevated so well by the fresh pesto and balsamic glaze. My sister remarked that the pesto was especially flavourful and we both enjoyed the olives too which came dressed with olive oil and garlic. Olives and Tomato Bruschetta (Image: Emily Stevens) For the main course, I tried one of the specials: the Cheesy Nduja Meatballs and Spaghetti. The pork meatballs were delicious; they were very well seasoned and had a melting cheese centre which I really enjoyed. The pasta tasted freshly made as well, and everything was brought together with a rich tomato sauce that had a bit of a kick from the nduja. Cheesy Nduja Meatballs and Spaghetti (Image: Emily Stevens) My sister was slightly overwhelmed by the size of her vegetable calzone - you definitely get your money's worth with this dish! She liked the marinara dipping sauce it came with and said the dough was excellent; it was finished with a bit of garlic butter and parmesan. However, she did say the vegetable and cheese filling could have been slightly more flavourful. Vegetable Calzone (Image: Emily Stevens) Despite nearly clearing all our plates so far, we decided we had to make room for dessert. I went for the Sicilian Lemon Meringue Pie which was the ideal way to finish. The meringue was perfectly fluffy and complemented the tart lemon filling and buttery pastry very well. Sicilian Lemon Meringue Pie (Image: Emily Stevens) However, I actually preferred my sister's tiramisu which was deliciously creamy and rich. It was a bit of a sweeter take on a classic tiramisu and wasn't overly alcoholic which we enjoyed. Tiramisu (Image: Emily Stevens) Both of us had a great time at Peterborough's Prezzo and will definitely be back. The menu had a huge variety of dishes, from classic Italian pizzas and pastas to different burgers and salads, so there is definitely something for everyone. Expect large portion sizes for main courses though, so be sure to leave room for dessert. Share
